He La now fully enrol and full of gratitude " THE NEW FEMINIHE HAROMETEII.—A new HMI altogether charming barometer has limn discovered by ma American profmeor. The instrument in question is nothing leaa than that fringe of .fuazy" hair keown in America en" bang," whiyh at present 1011,, fashionable adornment of beauty's forehead. The professor has found out that on the approach of wet weather thy" hangs" of dark.haired girle obstinately refuse to crimp, but lIERH down straight and limp while the hangs of fair auburn" are entirely unaffected, though these are endued with the equally wonderful property of becom- ing stiff and bristly when there is thunder in the air. This 1,, of couree, a delightful discovery but it appears to have 010 w drawbacks. Of course a conscientious man who gnee in for meteorological observations with enthydaan ought properly to marry his harometer. Then, again, he has first to Eltell his Iltlif i and though the lady allay come to him with a " bang" of one kind before inarriage, she may change to woe if a different sort afterward. It must be puzzling, too, whether to .docide upon the tearful barometer or the thundery variation. The latter would be useful to indicate the :approach of dorms, (specially if preceded by squalls ; but the former would be Imo inclined to variation. As for barometric preeaure—say in the case of a new bonnet--orm would be about equal to the other. On the whole, we are not disposed to look with favour on this latest "glass of fashion." The objection that, having once chosen your barometer, you cannot change it, mast always be an insuper. able one. besidm, europising your barometer does not care for you, what is there to prevent her, if a rainy instrument, from • anizzling ?"—llemo Folks. EXEHOTUIVEIONS Or alynony.—We tend to moject our present modes of experience into the past. We paint our past in the hum of the present. Thus see imagine that things which impressed no in some remote period of life must answer to what is irnpresive iu our present stage of mental development. FM example, a person recalls a hill neer the home of his childhood, and has the conviction that it was of gnat height. On revisiting the plam he finds that the eminence is quite insignificaat. Flow can we ac- count for this? For one thing, it is to be observed that to bia undeveloped childish nuncios the climbing to the top meant a considerable expenditure of energy, to he followed by a senm of fatigue. The man remembers thme feel inga, and unconsciously reasoning by present experience, that is teeny by the amount of walking which would now produce this sense of fatigue,simaginea that the height was vastly greater than it really WEE. Fnwn this cause arises the ten- ( ency generally to exaggerate the impressions of early life. `.'outh is the period of novel effects, when all the world is frmh, and new and striking nnpressiorm crowd in thickly on the mind. Consequently it takes much less to produce a given amount of mental excitation in ehildhast than in after life. In looking back on thin part of onr history, we remll for the most part just thom events and scenes which mostly stirred our minda by their strangeness, novelty, Ac., and no impressed theinmlvm on the tablet of our memory and it is this sense of something out of the ordinary beat that gives the characteristic Colour to our recollec- tion. This being on, we unconaciouslo transform the paet occurrence by reasoning from our preaent standard of what It impressive. Who hue not felt an unpleaaant dis- enchantment in revisiting some garden or park that rimmed a wondr,us paradin to his yam, eve..? All our feelings are cap.ible of leading us lido this kind of illusion. What seemed beautiful or awful to us as children is now pictured in imagination as corresporaling to what moves our mature minds to delight or awe. People who,, little outshone our own circle of friends, perhaps, in style of dress .ind living, seemed Inn. as children little short of princee and prin. came. Could we actually me them with our present eyo, we ehould, alas„ no longer find the glory in which our young fancies had enmrcled their heads. While the past may thus Coke an illusory hue from the very changes which our emo- tioaal life undergose, it becomes still further tramformed by the idealising touch of a present feeling. The is m familiar O fact as hardly to need illustration. Our emotion. of love, of remrence, of wertbetic admiration are artists that employ the past m a kind of canvas, for the emrcise of their imagina- tive *ill. We instinctively tend to Idealise the objects of it pmt love. The old rule de mortins bonurn has fomdationa deep laid in our emotional nature. It In much the same with Me emotiom of beauty and eriblimity that attach to objecta of inanimate nature sa well or, to human being.. Even a painful emotion, as resentment and hatred, may to some extent effect this result of transforma- tion. By dwelling habitually on the wrongs done us by an old friend, and forgetting all the good things we know ef him, we may come to transform thia person Into a monster very unlike the reality.—Frona..M.fiono of MmterY." on dole CcshoU Noyas.in e for April

Tan Note, 13F.FOlt8 inn Burrus OF AGINCOMIT.—The night before Agincourt was ,lark and rainy, and to the toil- worn English it wan one of hope and few, for 100,000 French lay there before then] thus the odds against them were as seven to one. Amid the darkness of the October night, and the sheets of descending rain, they could see the whole landacape glittering with the watch-firm of the French and fre meet bursts of their laughter and merriment were lwrne the pesing wind, from those who were grouped about these tires or time, Isamu, as they fixed the ransoni of the English king and his wealthy barone. As for the common salick a. they were all to be put to the sword, without mercy. Confident in their overwhehning numbers, they never colt. dived the possibility of doted; yet c.ould they forget that they were posted within but a few hides of "Cressy I As inen who had staked their lives and tlie warlike honour of England on the incur of the conking ,lay, the soldiers of Henry sp st the night in repose, in making their wills and confesdons, and preparing for battle with that gravity, order, and decorum which have ever been characteristic of British troops. The King himself took but little repose. , lle visited the different quarters of the arinv, end, duriiig a I elf season of moonlight, sent certain E.:tit:sins of skill to esamine the ground ; and, to keep the hearts of the men cheerful, he ordered the trumpet, drums, and fifes to play at intervals during the night ; but history fails to record the airs by which he sought to recd the memory of their homes, or the deeds of other days. So the night paw., away ; the Fren.K watch-fires died out, and the dawn stole on—the dawn of that great Feast of St. Crispin, the 25th of October, 1415.—" livilirh leuales eo leaal aad Sea." CArnm. or Crinnauraw—lt woe a sudden inspiration which induced Sir George Hooke, as he lay, with a Con, Lined feet of British and Dutch ship, inactive off Tangier, to nuke a dash at the great Spanish fortress on the oppmite side of the StraiM. Reports, which proven well founded, said that Gibraltar was but weakly garrisoned, and that its defences were wholly inadequate to tireteCt it from a vigour- °. attack—a bold and sudden descent might wrest it, therefore, from Siwnish hands. Accordingly, upon the Isl of August, 1701, the fleet appeared in the bay, and sum- moned the place to surrender. A certain Don Diego de Salinas was its governor, and It, had at his dispo,al just 80 regular soldiers, to which, by great exertions, he added a few hundred volunteers eel militia. With these, all W- armed and ill-found as they were, and with but few guns and small stereo of powder and shot, he made what chow he could; but the British blue-jackets and marines, landing at three points—at the Old 313,1 New Moles, and at a bastion now known as " Jumper's," from the naval captain of that mune who here led the am:milt—carried all before them. A 5 a last resource, the nuns of Santa Clara, followed by crowd of women and children, went in procession to the shrine of the Virgen If, Europa, to intercede for divine in- tertiosition ; but they fell into the hands of the enemy, who had by this time made themselves meters of the New Mole. Successful also at other points, Don Diego had no alteruative but to mpitulate and haul down his flag. The captors then book form.l possession of the place in the name of Prince George of Hesse, who ellA present, and who claimed the flume of Spain. But it was the Union Jack which was hoimcd, and which, by the ukumnctified doctrine that .‘ might is right," has continue' to wave over the rock of Gibnkltar from that day to this.—"Pietureagne Europe." Tee use or Trds en Tkowv—Though authorities differ as to the quality and quantity of tea drunk by the Tibetans. it is undisputed tlmt it constitutes their principal beverage morning, noon, and night, and that most ..f it comes from the province of Se-chuen. Deprived of the costly but in- dispensable stimulant, he stifle, from headache, grows nercous, restleas, out SI condition, and altogether unhappy. In outlying districts mothers are careful to keep the seduc- tire beverage from their children for fear led they should grow up unable,on occasion, to go withont It. And yet, to European taste, the infusion, as prepared by the Tibetan, is the remotest possible imitation of tea. The Tibetan tea- pot ha wooden churn, 1011CII liken butter churn, into which the boiling infusion is poured through a strainer; a little salt is added, and some twenty strokes appliel with a dasher pierced with live holes. A lump of butter is then thrown in, and the compound is agatn churned with from 100 to 150 strokes, administered with much precision and regularity.. The tea k then ready for drinking. It will be rem irked that, with the substitution of alit for sugar, the Tibetan prepara- tkon in of much the same composition an the tea drunk in England ; but the presence of salt is not perreptible, and Mr. Balder could detect no flavour of tea. It is impossible accurately to describe the taste of the infusion ; but to force a comparison, it is something like weak English tea with rich milk, but without any sugar or tea. And yet nobody would mistake it for milk and water, Mill less for butter and water ; for the tea principle affects the flavour, while itself becoming modified into sonie un-tea-like aetringent. flit evident that astringency is the property desired, weingthat many thousand Tibetans who cannot afford tea use oak bark in its stead. The teacup of the Tibetan is a wuelen bowl, not seldom an object of high price and elaborate workman- ship cased in precious metals:lnd encrusted with jewels. I. this he allows the tea to stand for a minute or two, and when the butter floats freely on the surface he blows it off into another bowl.—" 7%e Countries of the World," le Dr. Ra%ert Brown.

On the 14th it was enin fainter, and even with the greid telescope the toil could only lon men ati a thin wisp extending east- ward. from the head for a couple of degrem. The head itself appeared simply 38 a faint nebulous mass, with a slight me- tre! condeneatiow It is impossible to my whether thia carnet is a new one, or one which has been seen ate former perihelion passage, uMil the elements of itn orbit have bees computed. and for that purpose further measures of its posi- tion are still neceesary." BRZATIIINO UNDER WATIM.—By Mr. Fleuses process any person with sufficient nerve, and who is accustomed to diving, can exist for hours benmth the water without con- nection with the surface. A special dress with to helmet in- dexing the head requiree, however, to be employed. The dress has much the outwoird appearance of that hitherto med. The helmet is entirely closed, for there is no pipe to the air above water, as 18 customary with ordinary direr,. The power of bre.ithing depends on mmns within the sphere of the helmet and otress. To understmd this, we must con- sider the compoaition of the air. A 8 iA generally known, the atmosphere we brmthe consists one-fifth of oxygen,oond the remaining four-fifths of another gas called nitrogen. The mixture of these two gases ice etrictly mechanical one they have not entered into any chemical combination. The oxygen is the supporter of life ; the nitrogen merely dilut- ing it, so to speak, too proper degree, for the purposes of our lungs. In breathing, the oxygen is partially lost by absorption into the system,. arid the exhaled air contains a large proportion of earlsorne acid or—to call it by Ito more molten nante—carbou dioxide, a gas which is a poieon to animal life. According to Mr. Fleusa's procesa, a continuoe, supply of oxygen is procured from the helmet, where it is stowed Inc compremed 133(0, the supply being regulated by a valve under the control of the diver. The original nitro- gen in the lungs remains unaltered, and can be breathed over again along with a due admixture of the nargen. The strange thing in the disposal of the deadly carbonic arid gaa What becomes of it? felt bubbled up through the water? No, for the oxygen and nitrogen would go with it. A well-known chemical action is taken advantage of by mooing the carbonic acid which is given off to be absorbed by caustic soda; the result being the formation of mrbonate of aorla. The caustic soda it contained in a small tin or ebonite case placed in the body of the deem. It is M sol a- tine, and confined in the porm of spongy indiarubber, which is perhaps the only soft material impervioue to ita corrosive action. A proper arrangement of tubing causm the whole of the exhaled air to pass through this case, which requirwo emptying and re-charging about once a week—supposimr hat the apparat. is In daily use. To sum up the mmns by which Mr. Ileum breathes in a dress hermetically sealed from external air o--Ile take, down a eupply of compressed oxygen gas, dilutes it with the nitrogen, which is naturally present in his lungs and in the diving dress when he pule it on, and which, remaining unaltered, he can, as we have already shown, breathe over and over again ; and by bring- ing the exhaled carbonic acid in contact with caustic soda, transforms the deadly gas into harmless carbonate of moda. —Chambon's Journal.

A VACILLATING Boot—My negro gardener came to me one evening in great alarm, and stated that his twin sons,' Along° and Chango, had taken out his gun that morning,! and bad been missing ever since. lat once loaded my rifle,: loosed my Cuban bloodhound, and followed the man to his hut. There I put the dog upon the buys' scent, following on horseback inyself. It turned out that the young scamps had gone on the trail of a large bear, though they were only thirteen years old, and their father had often warned them not to unaldle with wild beasts. They began their adventure ' by hunting the bear, but endul, as often happens, in Laing hunted by the boor, for Bruin had turned upon them, and chased them no hard, that they were fain to drop the gun and take to a tree. It was sycamore of prculiar shape, sending forth from its wem many small, but only two large, branches. These two were some 30 feet from the ground, and stretched almost horizontally ill opposite dircotions. Tony were as like each other as the twin brothers them- selves. Chang° took refuge on one of these. Mango on the other. The bear hugged the tree till he had climbed as far as the fork. There lie hesitated an instant, and then began I to creep along the branch which supported Chmtgo. The I beast advanced slowly and gingerlv, sinking his claws into the bark at every step, and not depending too much upon his balancing powers. Chango's poaition was now far from pleasant. It was ueelms to play the trick—well known to bear hunters—of enticing the animal out to a point where the branch would yield beneath its great weight, for therewas no higher branch within Chango's reach, by catching which he could save hi cell from a deadly fall-30 feet sheer. Three more steps and the bear would be ujmn him, or he would be upon the ground. Braveas the boy was, his teeth chattered. At this moment, Mango, moved to heroism by his brother's peril, moved rapidly from the opposite limb of the tree. Stepping behind the bear, he grasped with one hand a small higher bough, which extended to where he stood, but not to where his brother lay ; with the other hand he seized the ani- mal firmly by its stumpy Mil. The bear turned to punish his rash assailant; but army as he was he turned cautiously. It was no easy task 'to right-about-face on a branch vitich had already begun to tremble and sway ben.th loie woight. Chango wals caved, for the bear evidently had tianeferred his animosity to Mango, whom he pursued, step by step, towards the extreinity of the other limb. But Chang° was not the boy to leave his brother and rescuer in the lurch. Waiting until the enraged brute was well erm barked upon Mango's branch, he pulled its tail, as he had seen his brother du before. Again Bruin turned awkwardly, .d resumed the interrupted chase of Chango. The twins continued their tactics with success. Whenever the be,to was well advanced on one limb, and dangerously close to one twin, the other twin would sally from the other limb and pull his tail. The ailly .imal always would yield to bin :atmt impulse of wrath, and coffer himself to be diverted from the enemy who was almoet in tin clutches. After two hours of disappointment he learned his mistake. He was now, for the tenth time, on Chango's branch, and very near Change. In vain Mango dragged at his hinder extremity ; he kept grimly on till Mango, forced to choose between let- ting go the brute's tail or the higher branch which enabled him to keep his feet, let go the foriner. Chang° could now retreat no farther, and he woe hardly a yard beyond the bear's reach. The branch was swaying more than ever, and the beast seemed quite aware that he might tax its strength too far. After • pause, he advanced one of his fore het a quarter oft yard. To increase the bear's difficulty in seiz- ing him, the terrified boy let himself down and swung with his hands from the bough. He waa hanging in rump.. between two frightful deaths. His heart was sinking, his ringers were relaxing. Then the deep baying of a hound struck his ear, and his h.ds again closed firmly on the branch. In a moment a bloodhound and it horseman sprang through the underwood. Chango held on like grim death— held on until he heard the sharp reiwrt of a ride ringing through the air held on till the falling carcass of the bear passml before his um held on till I had climbed the tr., crawled along the branch, and, grasping his wearied wrist, had assisted him to get back to the fork 1 the tree, and rest a bit. If that hem had only undemtood in time that ahoy in the hand ie worth two in the bush, he might have length- ened his done and gone down with honour to the grave ! By F. Blaie Crofton, in SY. Within twenty-four hours last week, in a dock of half- bred ewes on Mr. Butter's farm at Colston, Cot/par-Angus, fifteen ewes gave birth to 38 lambs, all of which are alive and doing well. Ten ewes had twins, four had triplets, and one had the unusual number of four. - .

Cvazons Cuvrrocastovs PrAN,—A fragmem of gneiss I was lately found by M. Behrens in the Tete Noire coverisl with brown-red spots of pulverulent matter. This was due to a small algal (ChrooPepus Jolithns, Ag.), consisting of a seri. of small thick-welled cells, whicharefound to contain I a red oil cooking the protoplasm; this oil sometimes exuding and forming yellow halls among the filaments. The algal in qu.tion lives on siliceous rocks where there are no organic matters; it must, therefore, be supposed that the protoplasm of its cells ham the power of producing. with water and the carbonic acid of the air, the contained oil. This oil evidently replaces the starch that is formed in the I green cells of other plants. The red coating of the rock I gicm an agreeable odour of violets from the oil in the cells, and the odour is retained for a long time, especially if the plant be slightly moistened. The name of IVA...in (or violet stone) is given to a siliceous rock of Brocken in the Liars, which ores its odour to the Chrroltpts Jolithr, Anon:mm.l. &tunes Cl.Assits.--Sir John Astley lately presided over a public meeting, held in the Corn Exchange, Lincoln, for the purpose of considering the jilane of the Science and Art Department for teaching the science of agriculture. After an addre. front Mr. Bucknuster, Sir I John Astley said when he first heard of the proposal he was not favourably impressed with it, because he could not see how it was to be carried out in rural districts ; but, after having heard what Mr. Buckmaster. had to say on the sub- ject, he had quite changed his minion, and he thought the classes proposed would he most valuable to Canters sons. Ile thought the landloids ought to take the matter up. If a class were started ill his parish he should certainly do all he could to persuade the young men to attend it. The diffi- culty which appeared to him was the want of competent teachers. A reeolution approving the object was unani- mously carried.

--LBIST:I.:I:I7HAL EDUCATION IN IngLeKn.—Tlie unesti.m of agricultural education in Ireland has assumed a very i mrlons aspect. We gather from the Irish papers that Pro- I fess. Baldwin has been allowed to retire on a pepsins, and tlmt there is a prospect of the agricultural department of , the Board of Education being dissolved. This would Iron serious blow to thc development of agricultural knowledge in the country, and unless we are much mistaken, the mea- sures now coTnmenced may Le productive of much injury to the material Iwognsa of Ireland. To thaw whose know- ledge of tho annitry extends a quarter of a centary back this assertion will appear rmsocable. That the system of agricultural education in Ireland has been of much good no one can deny. Although for from perfect, the evidences of improved farming in that country ore very apparent, and this is what one should expect. The agricultural Att.:6li and model farms throughout the country—in many cases hmk.l Of 00 with much disfavour—were certainly examples I °knot for imitation or avoidance, and kept the attention ' directed. The giving a technical education to a people is slow work, and tha.full results suust not be junked for in one generation. The young men educated at the Glasnevin Agricultural College are largely distributed over the country, either fanning on their own account or acting os hash& or stewards for landed proprietors. Well trained in scientific and practical knowledge, these men should be considered centrm of teaching for the districts wiser° they were placed. We we in England a just desire to encourage agricultural teaching. Let us hope that Ireland will not be treated to a measure of retrogrmaion, and that the large amount already expended in developing a system will not he sacrificed.— Ayricalteral Garate. It is.admitted universally that it goad education is most useful acquirement in any businem or profension, a nd renders the possessor, when he utilises his talents aright, a iflare useful, contented, and prosperous nun than he would Le if hii,‘,!_ducatioi: had been neglected. . . .

There :re .fe;;-o;-c-u-PatiTn's-O7. profeesions that require 0 knowledge of to many sciences, both theoretialy and prac- tically, an farming, and there is the practical experience and a practical knowledge of details that should be acquired by tuition under tne superintendence of some farmer who is generally recognised 49 an able and successful cultivator, breeder, ard general fare, nunager, or acapaired at none agricultural college to which there is a farm attached, ex- hibiting the most approved methods of cultivation and management. . . .

--I at-1.17:i now enter into the reasons why agricultural education has been torn I, negleeted,espemally in England. For while au excellent system of agricultural edumtiou is administered under Government supervision in Ireland, England in this rmpect has been neglected. Of course there is the Agricultucd College at Cirencester, but tenant fanners do not seem to appreciate as they ought this moat excellent end well-conducted establishment, for obvious reasons. lii, just the place to send the cannot tenant farmers; but what is one college among so many counties, and such a large country as England is, with its various soils and climates. Almost every province on the Continent has its Agricultural College and farm, and Ireland has most forty model farms scattered over its length and breadth, more or less under the control of Professor -laid- win, the Government Director of the 6lacnevin klodel Farm, near Dublin. There are alsoabout 170 National Agricultural Schools, at which schoolmasters give practical lessons on gardening and farming to the school children. In Ireland there are causes, without existence in England and Scotland that render the good effected by this system of Government agricultural training not so apparent and advmtageous as it would undoubtedly be if administered in Great Britain. Still, it is universally admitted that the Agricultural Model Farms have successfully obtained the objects for which they were mtablished, having exercised a very benedcial in- fluenceou the native agriculture. The Royal Agricultural Socieliesof England and Ireland, and the Highland and Agricultural Society of Scotland, have gent considerable impetus to agricultural education by annually ex:intining agricultural studentn upon a prescribed curriculum, and granting the successful competitors certifi- cates or scholarships. The middl,class schooLs to which tenant farmers generally send their sous have heretofore principally confined their attention to commercial subjects, but by the annual grant of ten scholarships of £2O each by the Royal Agricultural Society of England to pupils at these schools, designed for the farming profession, who succeed in the competition upon: agricultbral subjects, encouragement will be given to the [imagers of them schools to introduce the Practice and Science of Agriculture into their curriculums, and lead to the appointment of competent agricultural instructora at these schools, and impularise agricultural knowledge. The modals and prises awarded to successful veterinary students will lead tn a more extended knowledge of the nature and treatment of the diseases of farm animals. And the honour of obtaining a life membership of the society should he sufficient inducement no large farmers or land agents to ob- tain the senior first-class certificate of the society. Altogether the Royal Agricultural Societies of the three kingdoms are doing a vast amount of good work iu the fostering care and the encouragement they extend to every phase of agricultural interest and improvement ; the only drawback is, that they are often more ready to give than their constituents are loath or receive. Hence their efforts to educate the tenant farmers are putial ,illLi ineffectual. !Many of the tenant farmers to-day cannot appreciate, since they do not understand, the scientific principler upon which farming should he conducted, and as the attempt at the up- plication of principles tlmt are not understood are usually , unsuccessful, many farmers therefore sneer at science, aria are content to follow the beaten track, while their land yields thvw a fair profit. .

N igorous endeavours should be made immediately to in- troduce agricultural education especially in all rural tricts, Co that the rustics may imbibe. satisfactory know- ledge of the scientific principlte upon which agriculture should be based, as it is very important that the children of the small farmer and the labourer should acquire this kind of knowledge, since they are not permitted to bask under the genial and benign influences of Royal and other agricul- tural societies nod edmotional schemes, unless they take the opportunity of attending the lecture. given, or about to be , given, to all who desire in rural districts, through the agency of the Government Science and Art Deputment, upon the principles of agriculture. In promoting agricultural education we should begin at the lower stratum, and not at the upper. Of course, the education of the upper and noddle classes is very commend. able, but to neglect the education of thcee who arc manually engaged in agricultural operations is reprehensible, and can not be sufficiently condemned. Farmers should encourage their labourers either pecuniarly or persuasively to attend the science and art classes on agriculture, or use a little pressure with the recalcitrant of those of an indolent (mental) disposition, as the act of learning becomes more and more distastefal to those whose early education has been neg- lected, or those who have ceased to use their mental faculties in the acquisition of knowledge. Without insWuction in principles they will nevec become educated, nor advance one iota beyond their preaunt system, or nmkeany improvements. Those who have a practical knowledge of farming and the treatment of live stock derive for more benefit from attend- ing lectures expLdning scientific principlen than these who know nothing practic.dly about it; since they ran immedi- ately grasp at what is meant, and can the more readily understmd the principles involved, so that the lectures be- come sipremely interesting, and what before seemed nays. teriona and incomprehensible if it was ever thought of, now becomes clear and highly appreciated, leading the inquiring mind onwards from principle to principle, step by step, until he becomes a new roan,. treasure to bit employer, rising by degrees toa h gher relative position. THE UTILISATION OF BLA,T FURNACE SIAli IN LEEDS.—A t few weeks ago some particulars were given in the Mercury • with respect to the utilisation of blast furnace slag at Middlmbrough. Amongst the varied manufactures of Leeds I toe the works of the Aireside Hematite Iron Company, Ilunslet, where some of the sing produced in the manuf.• tare is utilise,' quite am effectually as is done at Middles- • brough, and with equally satisfactory results. The slag, • which formerly was thrown away as waste, is specially pre- • pared and broken into various sizes. It is mixed with a • proportion of cement, is moulded into a variety of useful articles,suiMble for builders and for other purposes, and can I be used instead of stone, being hard and durable, resist. • frost, and Like, a fine polish. The concrete is moulded in • the workshop,where it is kept for a few days, and is then • placed in the open air, doting and becoming hard from ex- • posure to the weather. The experiments at the works with this material have extended over five years, and some excel- . lent looking articice are produced, which cost much less than stone, effecting a saving in some instances, when compared with that material, of from 20 per cent, tti 50 per cent., ac- cording to the dmign produced. Ornamental work can be made too certain extent, and heavy flags, steps, and land- ings, Sin. thick, are turned out. The surface is as rin.th as marble; it can be left rough, if desired, or formed info,, pattern. Bay windows are made,as well as fireplaces,mantel- pieces, window heads, sills, string courses, sinks, corbels, hearthstonce, and a great vuiety of other things; the garden edging, with either round or (square corners, tie- ing much in request. The special advantag. are uniformity in quality and strength. Articles can be entered to .it a given position or place, and there is rIo further trouble or expense, as they can be taken direct from the works and placed in position. Compared with stone, which has to be worked with hand, the cost of this concrete is roceiderably less, and it readily takes paint. A gentleman in Leeds has had a skating rink made in his garden, surrounded with a narrow edging, and when frost prevails in the winter time the rink is covered with a titan layer of wamr, which frescees, and thus, both in winter and summer, his family can enjoy themselves in the open air. This is only one of the many ways in which the concrete can be utilised. Having satis- fied thenaselvm of the commereLl value of the slag to form concrete, the company sell it out to any one who wishes to use it, .d in thie way it is coming into general favour, and is being employed extensively for the floors af buildings, footpaths, and other purposes. The concrete tilm made at the works are rough and uneven on the under-side. and when laid in damp places they are found efficacious. The broken slag make. excellent garden walks, it becomes solid and cent. , pant is cleanly,.d in the country,where the varied colours of the slag can be seen, it is very pretty. The Midland way Company have recently ordered a quantity of round- • edged landings, made of "this concrete, for one of their • stations, and the company have the satisfaction of knowing • that the waste product of their works has been made to serve • useful public purposes, and to yield a return on the outlay. It has also been demonsmated ae theworks that glass bottle, can be trade of the slag, but this has gone no further than experiment. New Tone, Monday.—A destructive gale has been rag- ing in the Western States, and also with great force in Miesoari, where half the town of Marshfield Intabeen levelled to the ground by a hurricane The ditria afterwards took fire, znd the property waa coinpletely destroyed. Seventy- eight person. are Raid to have perished in the destruction of the louses, and MO to have been more or less injured. Ettelities are reported from other towns in Missouri, also mum' by the falling of houses. Further details fully con- firm the extent of the disaster, where only fourteen house. new remain standing. Seventy-eight persons have been killed, and a number of others are dying from injuries w- ceived riming the gale. Many am missing. and hundreds of families have beim rendered homeless. Surgeons and other sasistance are being sent to the sufferers from all directions. If is feared that many have perished at other places in Missouri. The hurricane has also passed over the North- Eastern States, through Wisconsin. Illinois, and Indiana, and across the lakes. to London (Canada), miming immense deetruction to properly and interrupting railway md trio- graphic commusiedion along its whole track. Later accounts of the destruction caused by the tornado in America state the number of persons billed at the town of Marshfield to be nearly a hundred. The Times American ' correspondent says eve-witnesses describe the tornado as frightful. It appeared era black cloud, funnel shaped, and lined with fleetv white, turning like a screw-propellor, with great velocity, destroying everything in its path. It was about hall a mile wide, and mount with a terrific noise, twisting off the larm trees and peeling the hark from the small trees, blowing the houses from their foundations, lift- ing cattle, hogs, horses, sheep, end poultry into the air, and carrying them long distances. ' The people of England have been called to pass judgment upon the acts of a Ministry which has neglected home in- terests to seek empty glories abroad, and iii. gratifying to mee that their sober sense has led them, in spite of some ern. harassing complications, to entrust the Government to other : hands The howling, of Alines, mob were mistaken by Lord , Beaconsfield for the voice of the English Commons It doee not seem to have occurred to bim, with all hislong and varied political experience, that the sentiments of the grealbody of electore are never publicly made known until theeleßlon day, and that he who would forefoot their strength and direction should take means to inform himself how the plain stay-at- home folk are thinking and talking. Tote lbatx.ox.—The Ballot Act is limited to expire on the 3lso December, 1880. It may be remembered that early in the late session Sir Stafford Northcote announced that it was the intention of the Government to introduce a hill con- tinuing the Act till December, 1881, with the view of having it thoroughly revised in the session of that year by a neer "Parliament." No such Continuance Bill was introduced, but it seems likely that the same course will have to be pro- posed when Parliament meets. The e notions will have brought to light many necessary amendment., in addition to those suggeeted by the Parliamentary Committce of 1878, sod there would hardly be sufficient time to consider them properly. The words of the 33rd motion of the Ballot Ant are J "Thin act shall contintie in force till the 31st Decent- her, 1890, and no longer, unless Parliament shall otherwise determine, and on the nail day the acts in the 4th, sth, and Bth schedules shall be thereupon revived." A reference to the numerous repealed act, in the 4th schedule, let alone the sth and Bib schedules containing acts relating to Scot- land and Ireland ouly, • ill show that the question, even if merely considered as a enactor of drafting, is not a eery easy one. A eimple repeat of the 33rd section would no doubt he the easiest course, but IT adopting it Parliament would lam the opportunity of pledging the Government to make the necessary amendment.—Larr

GlA.Deetielt AND TOE CONOIMATIONALITe9.—The following resolution was unanimously adopted at the annual meeting of the Wercestrrshire Association of Congregational Churches held at Worcester, on Tuesday :—" Thin Associa- tion of Congregational Churches forth° county of Worces- ter record. its devout thankfulness that the constituencies of England, on being appealed to, hare unequivocally con- demned the foreign policy of Lord Beaconsfield's Govern- ! ment—a policy which alike ignored the claims of natural justice and the opinions a Christian morality, and that ; there is now a prospect of a Liberal Arninistration under which civil and religious omality will be promoted at home, ; and the policy of England abroad founded upon principles of international justice and extension of freedom to oppressed ! nationalitiee, and this Asseffiation, while it would heartily rejoice should Mr. Gladstone return to the Premiership with he vacated tie years ago, acknowledges with gratitude and admiration his public abours, which have so materially contributed to the advancement of the Liberal cause in this country and further, this meeting having just heard that Mr. W. H. Gladstone and Mr. Ci. W. Hartrup have been returned for East Worcestershire, has received the intel- ligence with the aincereet pleasure,as still further increasiog the Liberal majority.' The xcretary was instructed to send the reeolution to Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone says in reply:—" Hawarden, April 15, !MO.—Reverend Sir,— Although time does not permit me tu tin AO much as acknow- ledge the numerous congratulations which reach me at this time, 1 cennot pass hy this agreeable duty in the case of the addrese which you have !wen no good as to forward, and for which I return too best thanks in connection with the eignal mark of coufidence just beatowed on my eon by the con- stituents of East Worcmtershire. But I must give a wider soope to my ackruprledgments. for I never can receive any teetinsoniai bran, the body to which you belong without feel- ing that it is rather for me than for them to testify, and that fern a debtor to them and to other bodies, in a position more or less similar, foe the generous sympathy and un- flinching steadiness and courage with which, during the last few years, they hewn maintained, through evil report, a cause now stamped—upon a regular appeal—with the national approbation. Ton are quite at liberty to give pub- licity to thin letter if you think lid—Pillow me to remain, reverend sir, your faithful and obedient servant, W. E. Gdens-rown."

'irtOld—AN CATHOLIC VOTT.—The following letter from "An Irish Roman Catholic,. in the rabid, will be read with in ereat ,—.Sir,—No doubt you have done your best to ' influence English Catholics to throw their weight into the scale in favour of the Tory Government ' We might have expected something better from the rehire. the leading Catholic journal, except that we remember how often the late Daniel O'Connell maintained that the English Roman Catholics were, as a body, a bigoted and narrow-minded clasa of politicians. It sense false and futile issue to attempt to put before English Catholics that by voting for Liberal candidates at tide election they would be doing what was detrimental to Catholic interest... This was a contrast on the broad lion, between Tore and Liberal principle, in the carrying on of the Government of the United Kingdom. You knew as well as anyone that it was to the action and triumph of Liberal politics that the Catholics of the United Kingdom were indebted for every 'shred of liberty and equality they now pomess. You 'crew that, notwithstanding the particular grievances we have yet to complain of and to labour to redress, we. as Catholics. enjoy more practical liberty at thin , moment in England, Scotland. and Ireland. than is enjoyed by our fellow-Catholics in any other country in the world and at thia day of our lives it in idle to insinuate that the advent of a Liberal Government iato office can bring with it the least danger of encroachment upon our interesm as Catholi.. And yet, forsooth.. bemuse there are many F:nglieh Catholics with Tory traMtions and proclivities,and because they live iu a little world of exclusiveneas of their own, the great body of English Catholics are told to follow the Tablet, and Lord Denbigh. and Sir C. Clifford, and to on—to shut their eyes to what their common sense tells them a/ Englishmen, and to accept their place in English parliamentary policy at the tail of the very Tory party, which has now been utterly and hopelessly beaten, in the teeth of the Tunes and the Daily Telegraph. Yore corres- pondent, Mr. E. C. firemen. in the Tail!, t of 10th April sreme to think it Ungraceful that such A candidate as Lord E. Talbot Mould have been rejected at Rumley by Catholic votes. May I ask what claims of a political nature had Lord E. Talbot to their noire? 111 am told be was the brother of , the Duke of Norfolk, I would merely ask—has the dual hon. of Norfolk always been on the Tory side? And even if it has, which I doubt very mord, why should the electors of Burnley prefer Lord Edmund Talbjt anymore than the electors of Midlothian should prefer Lord Dalkeith I Sir, I hope see good effect of the election will be to infuse more backbone into the political minima and action of the English Catholics."

Ile had wen with gratification to what an extent in this great county and among this excitable popula. lion the spWit of tranquility and the respect for law and order had prevailed. He thought that if those of them who were strong Conservatives would try to understand what were the motives of the Liberals, and if Liberal, instead of denoun- cing Cons, olives as stupid and dishonest, would try to believe that they were men who hal a love to see England great, we should be spared a good deal of that bitterness and extravagance of denunciation which sometimes threatened to inforn an eletnent of difficulty and danger into our electoral system. Tem LICENSED VireescLens AND TEE REcnrr ELECTIONS. —Mr. George Candelet sends the following letter to the papers : Perhaps you will he good enough to allow me a portion of your space to make a few passing explanatory and suggestive remarka on the action of the trade luring the ' recent elections, as various reports are afloat relating to the course pursued in 1890 comp tred with 1874. Shortly be- fore the recent dissolution a letter was adoressed to me by the Right lion. E. Knatchbull-Hugeesen, M.P., who, no mat. ter whether in or out of office, has always been disposed to advocate justice being dealt out to us fairly. This letter earnestly advised the licensed victuallers generally to avoid a trade combination against Liberal candidates, and to vote according to their political convictions. This document, I need scarcely say, was considerately received as advice from a friend. The reasoning of the right hon. gentleman, it is only right to say, was clear and intelligible, and was widely circulated among many constituencies, .d from my own pelpnal knowledge WIS accepted and acted 'pon with few exceptions to the advantage of the Liberal candidates. We are, therefore, in hope generally the Liberal party will, during their coming term of power. Drool extreme and hostile legislation of such a character as that which was resorted to prior to 1874. If any attitude of moderation is manifested by the new Government towards the trade, I venture to hope the day is not far distant when the rule of acting at future elections in a combinal form will become exceptional. The rash and violentattacks which have hitherto been mode upon the trade has, from my long experience, caus!,l the trade at past elections to do that from necessity winch was note matter of choice, considering the interesta involved. I there- ' fore venture to hone that the moderation which Mr. I Hugefteen has succesafully encouraged arty be strengthened, so that the licensed victuallers and beersellers may teem to feel that they have friends on both sides of the Rouse of Commons. _ _

QVAHERS tee PaneLIAIIMINM—In the new Parliament there will be found eight or nine members of the Society of Friends, and in that number are included for the first time two ministers of the denomination. There has been a great change in the relations of the Quakers and the House of Commons in two centuries. In the early days of the body one of its prominent member, was brought to the Bar, ad- judged a blasphemer. and, in spite of Cromwell's wish, branded, Burnt, dogged, and imprisoned ; whilst milder Ter- !ions of these persuasives to conformity were inflicted on j others. Under Charles the Second a temporary respite wee : gained by the Quakers, and the "lobbying" of Penn under Joni. the Second induced toleration. After the Quaker mind nod turned front Pennsylvania there were attempts to ' induce influent.l members of the body to become candidates. When the bill of 1832 created new comtituencies, 01, of I these delighted to honour the "Peat Quaker member of Par- j Bement'. who took his seat—the late Jimeph Pease, of Dar- lington, who WAS successful in his labours to develop his I native county by railway and colliery enterprise. llamas . emphatically the popular candidate in the new constituency of South Durham, and was triumph.intly returned. He entered Parliament on Feuruary 8, 1833, w. tendered the usual oaths, and refused them. On the proposition of Lord j Althorn, a committer was appointed to inquire into prece- dents, ant it happened that before this committee the me of Mr. Pease was pleadml by a Quaker barrister, the late Mr. John Hodgkin. On the report of that committee Mr. Pease took his seat, making the usual affirmation. It in not gene- rally known, however, that the qumtion of affirmation was again raised in the House. In May of the mine year the members of the Coleraine Election Committee came to the table to be "sworn," and the Speaker called attention to the case of Mr. Pease, asking if his affirmation was to be re- ceived in all cases. Amongst those who took part in the conversation that followed were Sir Robert Pert and Mr. O'Connell, who were in favour of such a course, and their advice prevailed, and the last bar to the admission of Quakers into the House was removed. Mr. Joseph Pease sat as mem- ber for South Durham till 1841 ; and before his death he had seen the seat he vacated filled by, first, his brother, Mr. Henry Pee the present president of the Peace Society; and biter ,y his son, the present senior member, Mr. Joseph Whitwell Pease. Another member of this family is returned to the new Parliament, Mr. Arthur Pease, the member for Whitby, and brother to the gpetteman net named. The well-known Quaker family of Fry is represented in the new House by Mr. Lewis Fry, the junior member for Bristol, and by Mr. Thealore Fry, the member for Darlington, who mkes the place vacated by his brother in the faith, Mr. Edmund Backhouse. Other boroughs which have returned Friends are Chelsea, in Mr. J. F. Bottoinley Firth Reuling, in Mr. George Palmer; Cambridge, in Mr. Wm. Fowler ; Hudders- field, in Mr. E. A. Leatham ; Mancheater, in Mr. Jacob Bright ; South-west Riding of Yorkshire, in Mr. W. H. Leathant ; and Birmingham, in Mr John Bright. Except in the instances of Mr. Bright and the late Mr. Chad. Gil- pin, none of the members thus returned have risen into office in the past.—Daily News.

T. POPI as-n ms little bit of the internal history of the Vatican has, says a Rome correspondent, made much impreseion in clerical circles. The son oboe of the Pope'e brothers bas recently become engaged to the daughter of a very rich merranti de Compaynn, to that generally wealthy class is called which transacts all the buy- ing and selling connected with the large quantities of live stock bred on the Campagna. The young man, unable to obtain from his father the meane of setting up an establish- ment fitted for the reception of such a bride, applied to his uncle, the Pontiff. All that the Pope could to for him was to give him 25,n00 iram s, which he was obliged to borrow for the purpose. The me—greness of this provision was much talked about, end Cardinal Pecci told the Pope the current gosaip on the subject. His Holiness replied that he was truly wry not to he able to do mom for his nephew, but that matters with him were in soch a position that he never had enough in the house for the necessities of the day. In truth Leo XIII. takes no thought for the morrow, but gives away all that reaches him as fast as it comes.

TIM Ton ihillkiE•Oz.xrea.—The inquiry into the Tay Bridge disaider was resumed in London on Monday. The inspector of the bridge stated that he beet found slits in the columns fire and feet long. Ile repaired the defects with iron bands bolted to the columns. Sir Thomas Hooch Melted the bridge and inspected the defects the Friday before the calamity. Its did not report defects before repairing. No one but himself, went to inspect the bridge. He had had no experience of ironwmk, and was tirst employed to inspect the brickwork. Number 4 pier girder was recovered on Monday. This girder encase' theguard's ran and second-class carriage, mad the ironwork shows that the rear part of the train bad been blown off the metals and grazed along the latticework. —On Tuesday several employes at the Cleveland Net and Bolt Company's works gave evidencx as to the manufacture of bolts for the bridge, and the non-inspection of their mann- facHire by the contractors. Mr. Henry La, CE., stated the result or his inspection of the bridge after the accident. He gave it as his opinion that the base of the pillors was too narrow for the strain to which the strusture was itable.—On Wednesday, Mr. Law, of the Institute of Engineers, wee further examined on tochnical matter'. tie referted coo- ' stantly to models, plans, and photographs, and stated the result of his calculations as to the pressure of the wind on the columns and piers of the bridge under varying condi- tions. His opinion was that the train was not blown from the metale, but fell with the bridge. Mr. &elder' Q.C. objected to criticism on the standing portion of the bridge as irrelevant, but the objection was overruled. The inquiry was again adjouraad.

Our special fresn Paris tells as how they feel in France over the result of the British elections, and we have hitherto heard how they feel in Germany, in Bumia—yea, even in Austria. His Majesty the Emperor of Austria is not happy ' about it. Geronay in reported as regarding it wick con- sternation, Russia with mild satisfaction, not l'aris with amialde delight. Paris wants to be at rest in these day, as togreat political combinations; she does not want to go to Berlin, nor does she combo have Berlin cmne to her. There- fore she is rejoiced at any evidence that anybody elno is to have this y.r rather less foreign politico than aerial, and that is mainly what she ems in Beaconsfield's defeat. For a people extremely angina to mint their own busi- ness, and very sensitive as to an unnecessary noise of warlike preparations in the neighbourhood,it is inconvenient and un- pleasant to have any national crockery shop near them invaded by • playful bull ; and thongh Lord Beaconsfield could net respectfully be compared to each an animal, vet he may fairly be compared to a wilful email boy, whOse heedless practice of going about and opening dons in a merely meddlesome spirit renders it prtsible t hat a hull may get in anywhere at any moment. Became his policy hall such poseibilities of danger in it the French may fairly rejeice that he is to be put dews and abaci ass great inter- national nuisance. It is sad to see how the people in Berlin are affected by Beaconsfield's fall. They believe the" peace of Europe would be much more amured " with him than without him. That they have shed tears we do uot hear ; but one despatch says they are trembling, and tears we sup- pom will follow. It is a little odd that both elements of the A ustro-German alliance are ci concerned in this event. Are , there any more secret treaties or steps taken to make them ? Was theta reason why the Emperor of Austria hoped the Con.ryatives would prosper? Viewed from our side the Atlantic the signification of these elections does not turn on any points such a those that account for the interest of England's European neigh- hours. Perhaps, therefore, we view the care more impartially tha others. Doublens there is much blundering in British government that, viewed in a narrow spirit, is to our ad- , ,antage; and on that ground we might wish the Tories to hold office for ever; but blood is thicker than water, and we I wood rather see a party of Liberal views and nound politics in power in England tlmn le prosper in a small /mirk in its defeat. dodged at our distance the result of the elections seems to be equivalent to the return of the nation to sober some in politics. It has had enough of capers. It has in- dulged ita fancy torn ph-Red foreign policy, and all that the phrase implies, and has found that there is nothing in it, except n dinappointrnent ad a heavy bill. It ha, danced a little and paid the piper a great deal, and now ills ready to Oct attention to the serious concerns of life—to take hold upon those nubetantial facts in a notional fabric upon the right shaping of which depends a great :State and a happy people, and set them in order ; to replace the confusion into which the machinery has fallen by mimeo and neglect with that vigorous ad eaey action which makes prosprtity. There is no country is which the two typical forces of modern politica are no plainly seen in actiun as in England. Conservatism and Liberalism fairly and honestly arrayed are nowhere else so definite in outline. In our own country the Liberal spirit frays out at the edge into the extrava- gant nonaenee of the Eearney party or the swindling spirit hardens at the other extretnity iota the mere greed of great corporation.. Unsettled conception as to the real There of politics is the source of all this evil. In France the political extrems—the only elements that have convic- tions on politics—are equally conapiraci. against the public welfare; and the mane between, the power that has nixie the present Republic, at once Liberal and Conserv, live, acts leas from tired convictiona guiding its conduct on points as they cries than from considerations of the premnt expediency of any propocal measure. In the three great countrien, therefore, in whmh a popular political ad con- stitutional system is in practical operation it is only in England that the limes erg so &finitely draw• that there in no proposition for an empire at one end or communistic nihilism at the other, in which the public morality is so felt in politics that the partly. are compelled to reject the alliance of factions that propose dangerous changes, and in which the party char/aerates are almost as plain as natural attribute, no that. given any Englishman's history, it in posnible to determine his party 'amain.. All the progressive spirit, all the viarous intellect, all the energetic elements of English life are Liberal; all the adhe- Edon to old institutions and old ideas without regard to their advantage, all the inherited dignity and nearly all the bilierited wealth, all the supercilious spirit of the nation and two-thirds of its arroganceare Tory. All the virtues Utile na- tion are not to be found in the Liberal party, nor all the vices, weaknesses and vanities on thather Nide; bin if the parties were analyzed llmroughly as to the elements of the national mind and clmracter to which they appeal it would be found that all that haa made England great and keeps her so, all that has led her out of the wilderness of feudalism Ily the sure path of constitutional freedom, came from the same impuls. that now inspire the Liberal party; and all tat has oppressed her people with tremendoa Widens of taxation and keeps many of them to-day inn condition of quasi slavery, all that hoe been an olydruction in her path to pro- urea, all in her policy and history that is a comfort to tyranny and injustice anywhere ha been Tory in origin and in epirit. To oise, therefore, the present rejoction of the Tories and return of the Liberals seem. more like the end aka political debauch and a return to Weary practices, than like the peril to peace that the Germans see or pretend to me in it. It is the function of the Liberal party to govern England and care for her red interas. It la the pretence of the Tories that they must take care of the world and let Eng- land take core of herself. There is in Una an ashlara, appeal to tke national vanity that has tempted it a great way, but the nation sees very plainly for the moment the farcical rather than the brilliantside of the Tory programme, and will find its way through the mazes of politics 011 the readier for that discovery.

(Front the Leeds Hem ry /reekty Svpp!mew ) There are two or three sufficient reasons why, in dealing with such a theme asChanges of Administration, the Cabinet of Sir Robert Walpole should come under notice. It was, in the first place, in Walpole's time that the First Lord of the Treasury became Prime Minister in name as well as reality. Walpole, as head of the Cabinet, held himself raponsible, not to the Sovereign, but to the Legislature, and through the Legisblure to the country ; and this ha.s been the posi- tion held, with more or lens eteadfastness, by the Prime Ministers of England ever since. IV,dpule also consolidated the Cabinet—so reformed it, in fact, that its members be- came loyal to their chief, instead of, as before, broken up by cabal,. It was during hes Administration, likewise, that the Act substituting 0 new Parliament every seven years wis passed ; and far hack as Walpole's reign now seems, it was then, and through the efforts of that statesman, that pro- wan given to the principle of Free Trade, although that principle was not to be fully developed until more thoi a century afterwards. Sir Robert Wallode's policy brought the country out of a wretched financial position, and his ob- ject in all foreign difficulties was to secure a settlement by diplomacy and not by the sword. lie averted wars abroad, and at home lie reconciled conflicting inter,sts and did much to extend the trade mid prooperity of the country. There are many faults to be found in his chequered mireer. These are matter of history. They are not difficult to trace, for of few English Administrations has no much been written. It is only necessary for the purpose of thi, sketch to show that Woiplo was really the first 'non who held the pooition of, Prime Minister, as that Neition is now understood that hio was the time really compact Administration and that some • him the attention of Parliament began to be turned for the first LIM, with anything like earnestness, simerity, and effect. to domestic concerns. The constitutional, the fiscal oral other reforms introduced daring Walpole's long tenure of °flies opened the way for much of the good work that has heen done by some of the Adininistrations of the ormolu eetdurY ; and they have a bearing, not too remote to be on many of the changes of Ministry that have taken place since the Reform Act of IS. It is with these changes that.tltretrospect deab.

The Duke of Wellington was be office during the last years of the reign of George IV., and his Administratkoi WAS continued when William IV. came to th,. throne. The clamour for Reform had then beconae serious. But the Duke would not yield, and the feeling of the country set ill against him. William IV. suceaded George IV. in June, 1030. In the November following, the King was to have visited the Mansi,o House but the popular tumult had by this time become to great that the visit had to be abandoned. For this the Duke was blamed. The feeling against hini outside noon made itself felt inside Parliament. Early in this same month of November his Government, faced by a combination of Whigs, Tories,and Radicals, was defeated on the Clod List. They accordingly rmigitral. It was then Novemkr. 1830) that the Administration of the Reform Act, with- Etrl Grey at its head, fiinge into power. In the following March, Lord John Russell intialuced his Reform Bill. Thin measure proposed the disfranchisement of sixty decayed boroughs, and the reduction of forty-seven others to a single Member mch. The people were delighted, but in the House of COMMOne the bill wan not received with enthusiasm, and as it only pamal the ,ermid reading by a majority of one, the Ministry decided one dissolution. The result of the appeal to the country was an unmistakable majority in support of the Government proposals. The Ministry therefore continued iu toffite. The new Parlia- ment assembled on June 14th. Ten days afterwards the hill was again introduced, and on the 21st of September it passed the Lower House by a majority of On. Time House of Lords, uninfluenced by the majority, rejected the measure. All over the country the indignation of the people at the action of the peers buret all bounds. In rood of the large towns there were disturbances such as had not been known sinee the Civil War. Apsley House wan stormed. The life of the great Duke was threatenal. Never. theless Wellington remained firm. He considered it his hay to opporse the bill, and duty with him was paramount. gate of feeling continual throughout the recess. When Parliament reassembled in December the bill was again in- troduced, and it passed the third reading in the House of Commoiw in Match, 1832, by a majority of 118. In April following the Lords gave it a second reading by a majority of nine, but non question of detail the Government were de- feated in committee bye majority of 35. There nose seemed only one course open. Earl Grey propowd to overcome the opposition in the Lords by the creation oft large number 14 new Peers. The King refused his assent to such an arrange- ment, and Rad Grey rmigned. The Duke of Wiiiiillolll *itll asked to form a new Ministry. Ile trial and failed. The for etc r Government Wor reinstated, the King now agreeing to assent to the demand made upon him. The Duke of Wel- lington and other members of the House of Lords thereupon solved the diflkully by absenting themselves from the Chamber while the bill was under consideration. The result was that the bill passed iM third reading in the Lords on June itti bye majority of 84, and three days afterwards it received the Royal Assent. By this bill Leeds was one of 22 new boroughs which were created to send two Members to Parliament. Earl Grey continual in office for two years more, when he resigned (July 9th, 1834) on account of secessions from his Cabinet, brought about by difference, relative to the government of Ireland. Lord Melbourne succeeded to power, but his Administra• tion (his first) was short-lived. Four months after he had assumed office, Lord Althorp, who was Chancellor of the Exchequer, became Earl Spencer, and the appointment of another Member of the House of Commons Chancellor of ! the Exchequer became neceswiry. Lord Melbourne waited on the King for advice in the matter, and was told toy his Majesty that the Administration must be considered at an end. Thus, for the time being, the Whig Ministry was broken up. The Duke of Wellington was summonod by the King. But the Duke did not again care for power. It is not to me," he raid, " that your Majesty must look for a Premier, but to Sir Robert Peel.," and he took the ground tlmt the head of the Government should not be in the Hon. of Lonls but in the Commons. The Duke added that he was willing to serve under Sir Robert Peel, and as Si. Robert was absent in Imly at the time, he agreed to under. mke the rmponsibilitv of the Administration until the new .r. •... •

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, APRIL 24, 1880.

Foe more than • week past the p 'laical world has been agitated with the problem whether the Sovereign ! would, on the resignation of the Besoonsfield Cabinet, send foe Lord Hartinglon, Earl Granville, or Mr. Gladkoue to form anew Cabinet. The metropolitan political clubs have been the scenes of considerable activity on the part of envious would•be office holder., and tho Loudon and provincial press have diecuseed and re-8..4.W the probable movements of Her Majeaty and the lender's of the liberal party in all conceivable aspects. The name of Mr. Gladstone has been on everybody's lips, and everybody hove been wondering whether he, the only Liberal alive who haa held the office of Premier, would be milted, and if salted if he would consent, to form • Ministry. By eommon consent the great Liberal victory is ascribed to him, by universal opinion the spode of the greateet electoral battle of moderq times are laid at him feet ; and there are few who dispute that Mr. Gladstone's rightful position is at the helm of affairs. The veteran stateeman, however, yearns for peace and root, but itis impossible for him to resist the strong current of public opinion that would carry him into elEce. It ha. been felt all along that he must be a pillar in the Liberal Cabinet by whomsoever it was formed, and the quee• Lion which has been agitating the minds of politicians was whether, though the Queen might send for either Lord Harlington or Lord Granville, the official leaders ! of the Liberal party, to form a Ministry, the duty ' would not ultimately fall to the let of Mr. Gledstone, : , the actual if not the official leader of his party.

These mu-mimes have to some extent been set at rest, for on Wednesday Lord Beaconsfield and the members of his Cabinet resigned, and on Thursday Lend Harlington was summoned to the presence of Her Majesty, at Windsor, on, it is believed, the recom- mendation of Lord Beaconsfield, wbo is strongly suepected of an intention, in making thic recommenda- tion, to perplex the Liberal leader& if not to bring a slight from the handa of Royalty upon Earl Gran- ! villa and Mr. Gladstone, hut particularly upon the , latter. Whether this suspicion is & groundlees and unjuet one only subsequent evente can establish. Something like studied insult was shown to Lord Hartington on his visit to Windsor, and the circum- 1 stance has ocaasioned no little surprise and comment throughout the country. For days Lord Besconafield has been tripping between London and Windsor attired in Isis richest raiment, and accompanied by his faithful body guard, Mr. Montagu Corry, now Baron Rowton. For him Royal carriages were pro- I aided, and his comfort and convenience atudied. When Lord Harlington arrived at Windsor, however, he found only one Royal carriage in waiting, not for him ! though, but for Lady Ponsonby. Through • heavy downpour of rain he walked to the Castle, and when he had lunched with the Queen, he was again obliged to face a drenching shower on foot to get to the rail- way station. Whethei this eliimourtasy is to be laid to the charge of Fier Majesty or to some of the innumerable flunkeys who sport in the Royal strum- phere is not quite clear, but the natio& will undoubtifilly feel that a snubbing was intended and given to the Liberal party through the person of one of its leader.. Lord Harlington, according toile rep ort to hand, declined to undertake the formation of a Ministry, and it is now expected that Lord Gren- ville will be asked by the Queen to undertake that duty. It is felt that Lord Granville like Lord Hai, tington realises the impracticability of being Prime Minister with Mr. Gladstone as a subordinate, and that he also will decline. Mx. Gladstone is generally understood not to be a favourite with Royalty, but he is the favourite of the people the people are mightier than the most potent of crowned needs ; and if Mr. Gladstone is willing to undertake the responsibilities of the Premiership all obstacles, royal and plebeian, to U. taking the reina of • government will be smothered by the swelling voice of popular opinion. Since the above was put in type it be been reported by one of our Metropolitan contemporaries that it was owing to a telegram from Lord Harlington that a Royalearriage was not in waiting on Thrusday, stake Windsor station, to convey him to the Castle. This much it is only fair to state.

Later telegraphic news brings to hand a message to the effect that yesterday both Lord Hartington and F.arl Granville visited Her Majesty, at Windsor, and that on their return they had au interview with Mr. Gladstone, who proceeded to Windsor by the five o'clock train from Paddington. The itiferenoe is that both Lords liartington and Granville decline to form • Miniatzy, and that Hoe Majesty has setth the nesee- sity of complying with the wishes of the people in calling upon the Gnat Commoner to be her Chief Minister ojf State.

This week election inquiry has been held in Liverpool, and though it has ended by oonsent of all the parties 'concerned in • withdrawal, leaving mat- ters jot Atalw to there hove been discloswee Masers-

_ trig; practices in modern eletioneerirag that are by no means creditable. In the election of town council- lors fur Abercromby Ward in November last, Mr. Stephens, • Liberal, wan returned, but Dr. Marsh, the Conservative candidate, petitioned against him, on the ground that there had been irreerularities on the pert of a presiding ollioer, and was Another contest followed between the same candi- dates in February. On that occasion Dr. Marsh was declared elected by a majority of 36 vote*, but on a subsequent scrutiny by the agents of both parties the majority was reduced to 36. It seae evident that on ; the part of the eupporters of Dr. Marsh corrupt prat- I trees had been resorted to on an extensive scale, and • the friends of Mr. Stephene petitioned against the re- turn of Dr. Martell. On Tumday, at St. George•s • Hall, Mr. Biron, Q.C., held a court for inquiry into alleged treating mad bribery. Mr. Segar appeared for the petitioners and Mr. Kennedy for Dr. Marsh. The evidence revealed the practice of wholesale eye- tematic personatioa, oh the part of the Ceuservativev, not only at the particular election to which the in. quiry was confined, but at the recent contest between Lord Ranmy and 31r. Edward Whitley for the por• liamentory reps:mutation of Liverpool. There can be no doubt, in the face of the revelation, of the way m which the Coneervative vi arcs were gained at the municipal and parliamentary contests in Liverpool, that in the late electoral battle in South-West Lanea- shire the 80-called Coustitutiou4 party trailicked as largely in un-constitutional practices as they did on the two occasions alluded to, and that the two eeate I for the county were secured by the old members by moan, neither justifiable nor oommendable. At any rate, there in good ground for rimpicion. The inquiry before Mr. Commiseiouer Brion revealed corruption of • type that thoee ou bride the .3ret circle had no con- oeption of. Vote often and early" appears to be the true difieition of the motto, •• Be tint and fear not," clamped on a h.dbook for the nee of Dr. Marsh's elmtion committee. How or by whom vet. were given, uslongastheywere given, war of little moment to the promotes, of the return of Dr. Morsh, One Joseph Shaw, a cab driver, reeidieg at 13, Lodge- street East, Preston, confessed to having had some experience in electioneering: he had "keen up to a little bribery ; " and he "sunk principlee when there ; w. • little money to be had." From this and. other , unprincipled hirelings the knowledge wee ex/ratted that rn.tOn has more than once furnished gulp of , pe.onaters to further the interest* of Limrpool • Conservatism.
