!! THE ELECTION RIOT AT WIDNES. At the Liverpool Anises, on Thursday, John Hewitt (on bail), Michael Hind (90). Peter Feeney (18), Patrick Moran (28). George Poole (33), Than. Lock (22), Ana James Carroll (26), all labourers, were indicted for leaving, at Widnes, on the 6th April last, together with ' divers other persons, unlawfully and riotously assembled 'lto disturb the public pea., and haying there canned • great ' riot and disturbance, to the terror and alarm other Ma- . I jesty's subjects. Mr. Heywood and Mr. Cooper prosecuted ; ' and the prisoners were defended lay 1/r. Commins —Mr. HeywooeLin opening the case, said lie was afraid it would Ibe imposeible for the (are not to see against which political party the carrot the mob were directed, but he begged them not to allow that circumstance to influence them in any I may. It appeared from the evidence that the disturbance ! took place on the polling day of the election for South- ! I West Lancashire. The polling elation at Widnes was in Milton-road, and the committee-rooms of both p,trties were dose by. During the afternoon, between four and for o'clock, a large crowd gathered in the neighbourtmal of the polling station, and it w. alleged that the pri.ner Dewitt came from his own house, carrying a flag, which afterwards I played a prominent part in the disturbance. Abut I tive o'clock Hewitt W.n in the centre of a crowd lin front of the Conservative committee-room, and Ihe was seen by n police inspector to rake up above his head the flag which he was carrying. The moment he did no stones were thrown at lb. ..Conservative committeeroom windows, and on Itie raising the flag a [se- cond time more stones were thrown. Hewitt then led Ike crowd through various streets into Newtown, a part of Widnes, passing on the way the house of a man named Smart. The crowd did nothing to Smarts house at that moment, Ind on getting oppoaite the boa,, of a man named Moore the prisoner Ilewitt raised his flag, and stones were thrown at the windows of Moore's boom. The crowd next threw stones at the windows of the Central and Mersey Hotels, and about seven o'clock they again came opposite Smart's house, and threw stones at the windows. A number of panes of glass were broken and the window frames and venetian blinds damaged. Later on the crowd threw more stones at the windows of Moore's house, oada nuniber of panes of glaas were broken. They afterwards returned to Smart's lonise, and continued to throw stones at the window. until about midnight, when theydispersed. While the crowd wer passing through the streets, Ilewitt was several times carried on the shoulders of some of the persons, and it was sLtted that when they were opposite Smart's house Moran shouted "let Its pull the hou. down. It is not built on a rock"; and Hewitt called out " Hurrah for the Liberals! Down with the 'Tories!" Cries of" Home Rule "wee, al. raised. It was alleged by the prosecution that all the pri- soners were in the crowd, and that they took more or less share in the disturbance.—Police-inspector Thomas Barnett, who wasone of the witnesses called for the prosecution, stated, in croes-examination by Dr. Commie., that he did not hear any cri. of "Cross and Blackburn° " on the day in question.—Dr. Commies: Then the Liberals had it Al their own way T—Witness They appeared to have it all their own way. lie added that the police did not apprehend any of the rioters on the day the disturbance occurred, RS the police were not in sufficient force.—Police-constable Clark- son, who was called for the prosecutors, stated that on the 6th April his inspector sent hint to find some member of the Liberal Committee, in order that the crowd niight ho, induced to go away,quietly. Ife met the prisoner Hewitt, and asked hint to get the crowd away. Hewitt said, " Yes. I will get a flag, and form a procession." lie afterwards got a flag, and tried to get the crowd to move on. A disturbance afterwards took place in the street, in consequence of .me- Way calling out that the Moo Smart had thrown something at the parish priest of Widnes. Hewitt tried to get the crowd to lee quiet, and said that he did not believe that Smart had thrown anything at the priest.—Dr. Commies, in addreseing the jury for the defence, urged that there was no evidence to show that the prisoners had a cotntnon object, or that they had combined to commit an illegal act.—A number of wit- nesses were called for the defence.—Thonms Smith stated that Hewitt tried to get the crowd to go away quietly, and when they did not do so he said, "If you are going to carry on this game, I wilt have nottting to do with you." The crowd "shouldered "him, but he wanted to get away. They would not let him do mat first, but when they let him down he went home. That was about more o'clock.—Other wit- nesses alsodeposed that Hewitt wantwl the crowd to disperse quietly. Witnesses also swore that Hewitt was in his own house by nine o'clock on the night of the 6th inst., and that he did not again go out until the following morning.—The learned Judge, at the conclusion of his suternhtg up, asked the Jury not to let recent political excitement operate upon their minds one mayor the other —The jury found all the . prisoners gailty of misdemeanour, and his lordship deferred

. _ At the Liverpool Assizes, yesterday morning, be. fore Mr. Justice Denman, James Manning (19), Patrick Smith (21), and Patrick Prendergast (27), labourers, were charged with having, at Widnes, on the 10th April last, together with divers other persons, unlawfully and riotously assembled to disturb the public peace, and with causing a great riot and disturbance to the terror and alarm of her Majesty's subjects. A third count in the indictment charged the defendants with ameaulting Donald Nicholson while in the execution of his duty.—Mr. Pickferd prosecuted, and the prisoners were defended by Dr. Commins, Mr.—lt was stated by Mr. Pickford that the disturbance took place on the Saturd,y night after the election for South-Weet Lancashire. A large number of people assembled in Marsh- street, and threw stones and brickbats at the police. Stones were also thrown at the police from the windows of houses and from courts in the neighbourhood In the course 011 k, evening, Inspectors Mayo and Barnett, who were in charge of the police force, being of opinion that the people were becoining very excited, gave orders to the police to charge the crowd. They did emend then atomJs and briokhatswere thrown at the police. The three prisoners took an active part in the disturbance, tel two of them threw pieces of brick at Police-officer Nicholson, injuring hi, head. Bricks and stones were also thrown by other per- in the crowd while the police were endeavouring to take the prisoners into metody. At the close of the opening statement of counsel, the learned judge remarked that there seemed to be a great difference between this case and that of the other Widnes rioters. In the present case the prkoners appeared to he individual members of a crowd which had no ringleader. The learned counsel on both sides held a short consultation, after which Dr. Comminssaidthat the prisoners would, upon his advice, plead guilty to the count charging theni with having assaulted Police-constable Nicholson.—By direction of his lordship, the jury found the prisoners guilty of the sesault.—Senteoce was deferred.

ELECTION RIOT AT PRESCOT. At the Liverpool Assizes, paterdav, John Murphy (29), Timothy Deveney (25), Richard Rotten (22), Thom. Max- well (34), Benjamin Tierney (17), John Tierney (25), Francis Mannion (43), colliers, John Sweeney (23), a labourer, George Collins (28),a labourer, and WillMm Aker (25), a painter, were indicted for having, at Prescot, on the 3rd of April, together with divers other persons le the number of over one hundred, unlawfully and riotously assembled to disturb the public peace, and then and there making a great riot and disturb- ance, to the terror and alarm of her Majesty. subjects. l'here was another indictment horning the pri. sneers will, unlawfully, riotously, and tumultuously assault. ing, beating, wounding, and illtreating Thomas Platt, Edward Range, Thos. Renshall, Wm. Jackson, and others Mr. Mulholland and Mr. Thompson prosecuted, and the ptisoners were defended by Dr. Conlon., Mr. On the night of Saturday, the 3rd of April, a Conservative meeting was held in the Assembly-rooms, Present, in favour of the candidature of Messrs. Cross and Blackburne. Some time before the hour appointed for the meeting large unmbers of people beg-an to gather in front of the Assembly-rooms, and someof the crowd were armed with large sticks. As persona entered the m•eting they were hooted at and jostled. A torchlight proce.ion had been arranges' to take place after the meeting, and immediately after those who attended the meeting came into the streei some torches were lit. The Crowd then be.me very disorderly, the torches were seised and extinguished, and blows were struck at many persons. Stones were also thrown, and the carriage in which Mr. Cro. and Colonel Illackburno were seated had to leave the town by a circuitous route. The prisoners, it wax alleged. took a very active part in the riot, and evidence was given to show that they had assaulted many ' peaceably disposed persons For the defence, Dr. Commins contended that the prisoners had not assembled for any unlawful purpose. Ile urged that this proved by the fact that there was no evidence to show that I the prisoners or any of the other people interfered in any way with the police. No actual disturbance took place until I , the meeting had terminated. and the torchoe were lighted by the supporters of the Conservative .ndidates. The per- sons who carried the tothhes struck right and left with them, I and 111 that the prisoners did was to defend themselves.— 1 A number of witne.es were called bv Dr. Comrsins, and , , they swore that the torchbearers were the first to create • , ' '' • '

FALI, POLITIOAL Renours.—The elder Disraeli, in his "Curiosities of Literature," writes thus X false report, if believed. during these days may be of great service to a Government. Thie political maxim has been ascribed to Cathenne of Medici', an adept in env d'etat, the arrana ioiprr'h! Between solid lying and ditiguised truth there is a difference known to writers (or speakers) skilled in the art of governing mankind by deceiving than,' as politics ill-understood have been cleaned, and as are all party politics. , These forgers prefer to see the truth disguised to the gross fiction. When the truth ran no longer be concealed, then they can confidently refer to it, for they can still explain and obscure, while they aecnre on their side the party whom cause they have advocated.- How suggestive to : D'leraeli the younger !

The precept of the School Board " will not ebew what corn is called for in respect of the principal of the I.ns, and the contribution of the township on account of the hr.es will not be • tined soot, as it will vary from time to time according to the rate- able value of the iownaltips included in (he united district. Several matters connected with the re- nnt election in Sooth-West Lane,,hite were discussed. The question of at once forming a Liberal Club in Eulestown for the district was warmly taken up, and, with a view of placing it in effective order, it was resolved to arrange for • visit from Mr. T. A hearty vote of thanks to the chair- man concluded the proceedings. Neweon CHORAL SOCIETY PANTY.—The members of this useful and pr,spering society, along with a large compiler of Friend. celebrates' the close of their first seasbn, bv a tea I party and dance in the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday last. There were about 100 at tea, a large proportion of whom were niembers, memberk wives, and the elder meni- bers of their families. The society itself numbers about 60, but the privilege of inviting a friend was given to every member, and the committee were empowered to issue invita- tion. ale°. The proceedings opened at seven, and after a really excellent tea, the room was speedily cleared for dancing. which was carried on with unflagging interest until between three and four the following morning. The Earl of Beaconsfield, who on Wednesday tendered his resignation as Print. Minister t Her Majesty, returned from Windsor Castle to London on Thursday by the ordinary train which left at • quarter to twelve. As the train dc. parted front the station the noble Lonl was loudly cheered by the numerous spectators who had assembled, and on hit arrival at Paddington he was also warml:r received by aeon. siderable crowd who had gathered on the platfarm. His ! Lordship at once drove to Downing-street. Her Majeaty having accepted Lord Besoonsfield's resignation, a royal messenger was despatched from Windsor Cast:e shortly after ten o'clock on Thursday morning, proceeding to Devonshire House, Piccadilly, hearing despatches front the Queen to the Marquis of Harlington. On receiving tier Majesty's sum- mons between eleven and twelve o'clock, Lord Harlington first communicated with Earl Granville, and then started for Paddington, which he left by the 1.5 train for Windsor. His tdrilviip, who travelled alone in a first-class reserved carriage, was cheered or the train paaselalong the platform. Windsor was reached at 1.55, and the noble Lord at once proceeded to the Castle, where he was deeived in audience ,bv Her Majesty. The noble Marquis left Windsor by the 415 train, having walked :midst a heavy fall of rain from the Castle to the railway station. lie was at once recognise' by the crowd who had ansembled in expectation of hi', arrival, and on the train leaving the station was heartily cheered, a compliment which he repeatedly acknowledged. Lord Hartington arrived at Padding- ton shortly after five o'clock, and at on, drove direct to his town residence. After a brief Way he procevled to ISt, Carlton Ilotoe Tesrace, in order to consult Lord Granville. Aft, his consultation with Lord Granville, larch Hartington, together with Lord F. Cavendish, visited Lord Wolverton, where a brief conference was held with Mr. Gladstone The Prete Association understands that Lard Ilartington informed the Queen that he must, with her Majesty's gracious permission, decline yr undertake the i ! responSibility of forming an Administration, and repre- tentations have been made to Mr. Gladstone which, it is said, will induce the right hon. gentleman to undertake the formation of. Ministry if sent for by the Queen.

......•—... Lord Harlington, in company with Earl Granville, left Devonshire House yesterday morning. shortly before clever o'clock. Their lordships naught the eleven o'clock train for Windsor. The departure of the noble lords for Windsor was unexpected by the railway officials at Paddington. The first intimation the stationmaster received being the presence of the two distinguished travellers on the platform about two minutes before the train started. Their lordships were searching for an on-occupied bent-elate carriage, and this being found for them, the noble pair settled in op- posite corners perusing the daily papers, in which on energetic newsboy had, by pushing his way into the carriage, induced them to invest. There were very few persons on the platform at the time. On arriving at Windsor, L.r.ls Granville and Harrington proceeded in one of the Royal carriages to the Castle, where the resolution arrived at by the Libe al leaders on Thursday evening was laid he.fore. the Queen.

A London correspondent, writing yesterday, says Whether Lord Harlington accepts the duty which fib Sovereign desires to impose upon him depends on the result of the interview which Iris lordship and his noble colleague Earl Granville are now having with Her Majesty. The situation at this moment is an open one, and the announce- ' ment of Mr. Gladstone being recommended Co the Queen is Cl any rate premature. Opinion in London is veering to the ' conclusion that under certain conlitions Lord liartington would undertake the task of forming an Administration. ' The personal friends of each of the three statesmen whose names have been so freely mentioned in COll. nection with the Premiership are wantono desirous of the appointment or their panicular leader, a• although whomsoever is appointed may feel aseuresl of the support of his colleagues, yet upon the abeolute appointment depend. many minor poste." On their arrival in London hoth drove at once to Mr. I Gladstone's house, in Harley-street, where all three remained in concultation for some time. At twenty minutes past four Lord Hartingket kit on foot, and at the same time Mr.; Gladstone'c cirriage, which had been Mending at the door, was sent avray. Earl Granville left Mr. Gladalone's soon after, and returned to his residence in Carlton-terrace, where be was met by Lord Wolverton. During the afternoon the Duke of lrgrtn milled at Earl Granville's, and Lord Wolverton and Mr. Adam had a long concultation. After Lord Harlington and Earl Gran, ille returned from Windsor Castle it was reported that Her Majesiv had resolved to send for Mr. Gladstone, •nd the report was con- firmed shortly before five o'clock, when Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone and Mite Gladstone drove to Paddington station. The right hon. geivtleman loft by the five o'clock train for Windsor, taking his seat in • tirst-class compartment specially retained for him. A large crowd had gathered at the station, who evincee the greatest curiosity to see thv veteran statesman, and a policeman W. stationed at the door to prevent the eager snectetors coming too close. Ringing cheere, agaia and again renewed, were given as the train moved off, a compliment which Mr. Gladstone acknowledged most graciously. l'he greeting at Windsor on I the right hon. gentleman's erriyal there at 5-35 pan, wan acarcely less enthusiastic. A Royal carriage was in waiting, 1 j and Mr. Gladstone was at once driven to the Castle.

It was a picture to see the fallin Minister's face during the Ueneral Confession, and when he came to the sentence in the nifical about the proud being scattered in the imagination of their hearts, and the mighty being put down from their stet, a great tear rolled on to his dainty little prayer book, and Monty Corry banded him the smelling salts. gir,—As "the mild season, that time When rain from above falling makes all thing. green, sod springing flowers awake from sleep and hail the wished-for day," invited to token walk, and the thus being convenient, I strolled into Burtonnood, or. as perhaps it ought to be called, Bowyer- town-wood. paosing the ruins of the mill erected by T.P.L., 17113, and under the viaduct, a picturesque object, AI seen from Newton Common, and on to Bradley Ilan (similar in ume and fame to that at Grappenhall) and once the moat bon. of the ancestors of the Ugh's, of Lyme, pausing to admire the springing flowers with as much seat ao our Norse forefathers, and after viewing the icy-grown ruins of the gateway, I turned my steps down the volley of the Sankey, good bon .shot to the ancient home of the Athertona, the ancient landlords of Newton, and known a, "Old Hen," a manor In.ose of 200 years ago, with ito maasive brick *wall, in excellent preservation, with nine windowe in front, built on a vantage ground above the valley, and calculated to withstand wind and weather for as much longer. The kitchen is minority capacioue, and the staircase. are wide and curious. In the been in the date 1730, on a tie beam. Within similar distance is New Heir and following the main stream would bring us to Winwick, which stands out from it, boner of trees. But turning to the east we pass Wargrave—a:place of some antiquity, if names go for ought —and the alains or Demesnes, of the ancient home of the Blackburnes, known aa Newton Hall, built in 1605, the year of Gunpowder Plot. It has the armorial bearings of the Blacklitanes, but not the grotesque wooden heads of the Old Hey Form, although it is much older. Passing under Newton bridge, and by the mill, we look over the bridge on the high -Coot to where the ancient bridge and smithy etul, halfway between it and the dam which confines the waters of the Siete. At the angle of the lake is "Castle Hill," a lollilescription of which will he bundle the Manchester Philosophical Society's Transactions for 1846, when the barrow wan opened in tho presence of local antiquaries ; anti when A footpath led across to liolhorne Park another reel- Fleur,. untie Leglis and there were remains of cottages thereabouts. A few hundred paces further epic the Dean bloor School, of date 1677. Pursuing our course up the high street from the bridge we paos the cite of another Flame,. Opposite to the entrance of the “Cockpit" School stood another still more ancient school,mentioned by liSfoe in his °ltinerary of Great Britain" and the "Blue Crows" of the District ; hut root and branch are gone, for helt, schools have disappeared in the lapse of thee, and the very ground the first stood opon has been hewn Away to make roong for a carriage drive. Adjoining IA the Church of St. Peter's, founded irg 1185 aurl rebuilt in LS3I, when the district wee provided with churchea in order to counteract the influence of dissont, and notably that of Crow-lane Chapel. The old coaching-house, .4 the older port of the town itself,are all cleared away. the one to find room for an addition to the church burisl ground and the ether to make way for Park- read. Pausing up the high etreet and by Rob-lone we reach the Sean School, and pause to think why it was ever called the Sean School, for there never was a deanery any- where near to it. At last it dawns on our intelligence that it is simply the school in the valley—from the Anglo. Bacon word .rienii, a valley. Yes ; there it stands to remind us that it still supplies part of the mean, for those lion," or scholarships about to be thrown open to deserving boys in our public schools in Newton and Earlmtown, but again, and to-day, for unknown mums, "postponed,. and Which postponement will be very mortifying to the lays, and to the parents of thooe boy, who are ready and 'filling to stand the test of examinations fur theee scholarship, and who most likely will have to go to work and let °them carry off the prices. We merely note this fact in a timid kind of way, and by way of protest in naming. and continue our walk to the Dean I mu, a nylvan reeort of the better sort, Ulterior only to the Lady Hill liam, where surely none but feria o veritable fairy dell, where" Bottom " might have been made in to an aes.—Yours truly, Newtonde-Willows, April 20, 1880. /111STICUS.

I believe "art culture" to be one of the beat antidote, to the vices and (Grotty of our them, by gi] ins greater scope to the intel- lectual faculties, and drawing the line of distinction inore sharply between] education and ignorance, morality and vice, and Imparting a loftier significance to all our aims and an- pirations Therefore the more opportunity there is given for the etudy, and perentit of this object, the greater and more permanent will he the benefit of a Free Librory to the ' inhabitants of St. Hole.. If then the encouragement of the Government is not easieled by our local authorities, if the Library Committee neglect to supply or with works that will throw light on the beauties and advantages of this amiable art," Sr as to recommend the etunly and facilitate the knowlidge of it, then the :ault will not rest with the people, but with the Antall, and indifference etch, Council. Be it understood that I do nut deprecate the reading of "light literature." There is alwayn hope for • young man who reads even stupid noveln Constant reading cultivate, tame, and the lower grade of needs are epeedily abandoned for works of a higher clam ,not net literature "is not to be obtained it is no use to complain that seventy per cent.of all the books taken from our library are works 0 fiction. I venture, therefore, to observe that the pottering economy, or esiltul stupidity, practised by the cernmittee in the selection and purchase of books (only fancy, • dozen boobs in this partieular clam) should give place to a higher and worthier spirit. connmennurate with the intelligence of a borough of the else, importance, and wealth of St. Helens—Yours truly, PSYCHE. Sir,—ln your moue of March 13th last, you inserted a letter from myself under the above heading upon the subject of the scarlet fever at Lymm. I introduced the name of Dr. Fox in that letter, and commented upon the fact of the sick chil- dren not being sent to the hospital. lam now told that Or. Fox feels personally aggrieved at the use of his name. but I non only reply that he was, to my mind, in for porentis in relation to the children, and the tiovernment officer in charge of the health of the district, and that he had full power to have acted as I thought it was proper that some one should art I had not a shade of feeling againet l/r. Fox personally, and to this extent I apologise to him, namely, that if I have regdrded hint as responsible, where he had no power to Oct otherwise than he did, I regret it. At the same time, I retain my opinion, that had the early cases been sent to the hospital, or otherwise isolated, en much loss of life would not have taken place.—Youre faithfully, W. ROBSON. vin,—Now that the excitement of the election is over the µwere seem to have log much of their intermt. There was something exciting and exhilarating about them during the election, but of mune now it i.e thing of the post. Old things have 11.1.11 away ; and to ! all things have lwmme new. There is no doubt, sir, that groat changes have taken place. It makes one pause and wonder at them; but how and by what means these changee have been caused remains to .ine a mystery. Many may nty the cause has been a revulsion of feeling against the liovernment of lArd Beaconsfield. No doubt it has, in a great sense. Others I may ascribe it to different causes, hut I contend that we have I to thank the Press for placing before at fairly and impartially the true position M which we and the country were placed.: Now we have three papers in Warrington. (octets it is the largest newspaper in the world, though I have now one near l me much larger, to that statement is not true. Its motto, I too, is Neutral: in all matters political and religious." Well, of its neutrality I will leave the people to Judge, and dismias it with a caution to both political partisans and to the religious element. The next is the all-important I Er,imiaar. Well, now, I think that the manner in which 1 the Examiner haa been conducted during the past few years,' by giving fair and honest reports of all meetings and expos- ing those things which so directly affect wan working men, has been in a great measure the foot. of the great change in the political representation of this borough. Inderd, it is generally admitted to be to. I have beard this opinion expreas.l at different times, that if you want a correct version of any matter relative to the good of the town, you must get the Exammer. A Conservatire gentleman, epeak- ing in a public room the other evening on the cause of the Conservative defeat in Warrington, said "The Ennui no, is what it professes to be; it sticks to professions honestly and fairly; and I tell you that you must thank that consistent paper for your late defeat." Is it not to, I should like to a.k Only newspapers of the neutral kind, and that trim their saila to any wind, care to blow their own leoonpnteu hut knowing. as tend many others do, the great assistance the Examiner bat given to the Liberal party here, I think it is only fair that in your case the principle of giving honour to whom honour is due should be observed. The worth of your paper is of great value to anyone seeking political knowledge, and from its pages I have culled many bright thoughtn and expressions. The result has shown others mutt Inane been benefited in a like manner—l twg to remain, yours, he., JOHN 911UFFLEBOTIIAM. 19, Winwick.road, Warrington.

THE CHARGE: TIM RIOTS AT PRESCOT AND WIDNES.— His Lorkship, in charging the grand jury, referred to the ! Widnes and l'rescot election rioters in the following terms: I —There are three charges against no less than twenty men in all, of violent ...tilts, committed in the course of Hots at election meetings, or rather riotous meetings during elec- tion proceedings and canvassing times, by violent throwing of bricks and of etones,and the are of sticks and flatters of that kind, at two places, I think Vildnes and Preacot. Now, it is perfectly desirable that I should just give the heads of the law applicable to such oases. lkfore you find a bill you ought to see a prima facie case established of theme things. First, there must have been at least three person. engaged M an unlawful assembly. They need not woes- partly nave been assembled in the first instance for an un- lawful purpoac. They might have been assembled in the first instance for a lawful purpose. but it would have been an unLtwful assembly if great violence took place, and if in common concert they were going about aiding and abetting one another M throwing atones at windows, wanking the police, or in matters of that sort. So as to make It an un- lawful assembly you must be adiafied that in each case before you find a bill there is a priaa facie case of its being an assembly of three or more in that sort of business— originally a lawful sasen,bly pos.ibly, but unlawful because of violence going on by three or four persona, snch violence as you considg to be u lawful with reference to what I am I going to point o.tit to you.. It must have been accompanied • ' •

violence, or at least an apparent tendency thereto—as . he calculated to iaspire people with terror, such as being armed, using threatening speeches, turbulent gestures, or Ike like. But in order to find a true bill against any individual it will not be enough that you ahould see a prima foci< cue merely of that individual being one of, say 300 persons, some of whom were doing such acts as those I have des- cribed. You ought to be satisfied at all events that there is a prima facie case that the persons against whom you find the bills were taking a part in the matter themselves, and were not merely , persons accidentally caught against their will ; amongst others who might be doing these things. Now, as far as I can see, the pollee—who are, of course, in such cases as these, principally the witnesses—seem in most C. 4.1., if not all, to have selected persons against whom there was a case of very violent limping, showing that they were taking a part in the unlawful proceedings, whether by breaking windows, assaulting the police, or throwing brickbats about—persona who seem to have been taking, priovr facie stall events, a part in the riotous pro- ceedings that were going on and if that is so, it will be your duty to find a bill, which would be investigated be- lore a petit jury, against any persons so conducting them- selvea. It is most important, I think, that it should be thoroughly understood that one doctrine, which seems to have come from the mouth of more then carol the par- ties who have been taken into custody, is a most dangerous doctrine, and utterly contrary to the law of this country, and that is the expreseion, which I think you will find was used by one or more of the persons who have been taken into custody—“ You cannot do anything to us kr this, for this is election time, and there iron lan in election time!' I an, quite sure you will not by any course of your, sanction any such doctrine as that. It will not do, cad it would be a most terrible thing if such a doctrine aa that were to pre- VAIL Life and limb, buildings and homes, might be semi- fictxl very readily lithe least sanction were given by any judge er any persm in the habit of administering the law, or whose duty calls upon him to do so, by way of sanction- ing such • doctrine as that. I think I have made all the observations I need make upon any of the cases. The cause list of the Ski Fri. Court contained 37 cases, of which 12 are marked to he tried by special juriea There were three actions against the London and North-Western Railway Company, one againat the Furness Railway Com- pany, and one against the Liverpool Tramways Company, Limited.

Ann Gibson, alias Regan, 213 years, of no occupation ; Elisabeth Basnett, 313 yearn, hawker and Dominic ltegan, 21 years, striker, were indicted for having, at Warrington, on the 24th of March, stolen with violence £1 15s. from the person of Peter Milligan.—Mr. BPConnell appeared for the prosecution.— The came for the prosecution was that on the evening of the 24th of March the prosecutor, who mass farm labourer, living at Preston Brook, went to the Patten Arnie public house, in Warrington, and there, in paying for some drink, ahovred sparer containing El 15s, which the two female prisoners had the opportunity of seeing. The prosecutor left the house, and was proceeding down o atreet, when the prisoners with others came up, and he alleged that while one of the women took him by elm breath, the other put her hand in his trousers pocket and took out his money' which fell on the ground. The male prisoner took him by the hack of the neck, put his knee in his back, and threw him into the ro3d.—The three prisoners were found guilty, and sentenced to 15 months' hard labour each. .

Aerrom AGAINST TAX LONDON ANT NORTHAVETI'PIiN RAILWAY Co.—ln thiscase the plaintiff was Joseph Swettle, master bricklayer, of Whiston, near Preecot, and he sued the London and North-Western Railway Co. for damages which . Ire alleged he had sustained in an accident occasioned by the negligence of the company's nervants.—Mr.C. MI , and Mr. Smyly appeared for the plaint,ff, and Mr. Q.C., and Mr. Page for the defendanth.-1 he plain. tin evidence was to the effect that he was a master brick-

layer, was 42 years of age, and had a wife end fourchildren On the evening of the 24th July last year he went to Liver- pool on business, accompanied by bin son, a lad of thirteen years. Having transacted his business lie went to Lime- street Station, and took third-class tickets for himself and.his not to Present. The train by which he intended to travel had, however, gone, and he therefore went by another, the 11-10 p.m. train to Rainhill, intending to walk thence to Prescot. lie and his son travelled in a third-class compart- ment, his son sitting opposite him. When the train wee approaching Rainbill and was "slowinhit he opened the carriage door, and on the train stdpping ot out. Turn- ing round, he took hold of the door wit left hand, and put out his right to reach a basket of cherries which his son was handing him. At that moment the train was suddenly started forward, and he, having hold of the door, was dragged along the platform for some distance, and then fell between the platform and the carriages. The wheels of one of the carriages passed over his left arm, alnaost severing it close to the shoulder. He turned himself over and then avoided the wheels°, the carriages passing over his body. In doing so the wheels cut off the thumb of his right hand and the tips of threw of his fingers. After being rescued he was taken home in a cab, and the next day was renioved to the Royal Infirmary, at Liverpool, where he remained about for weeks. l'revious to the accident his business earnings amounted on an average to £2 las, per week. The plain- tiff was cross-examined at some length by Mr. Gully with a view of showing that he alighted before the train stopped, but he denied that he did at, and still maintained that the train after its stoppage sud- denly " jerked" forward. Witnesses who were travelling by the same train ae the plaintiff were called, and bore out his sattement—The defendants denied the negligence, and pleaded that if there teas negligence on their part there was contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff in alight- ing from the carriage before the train had stopped, but they relied mincipally upon the point that the accident was occa- sioned by the plaintiff's own negligence. On the part of the company a number of witnesses, including the driver and guard of the train, were called, and tilt,' denied that there was any temporary stoppage ore eubacquent "jerking" for- ward. One of the passengers by the train was Mr. ta". H. Stirrup, manager of Ike Britannia Glassworks, at Rainbill, who said that the train gradually slackened at it approached the station, and finally atoms] without "jerking" on again. The next morning he went to the railway station loam the /nears is cm, and there found marks of where plaintiff htd been dragged 17 yards along the gravel—The jury found that there was no negligence on the part of the rail- way company, and consequently gave a verdict for the •fenclants.

div.head: BOLD FARMER HEAVILY FINED FOR CkIELTY TO ANIMALS.
div.p: A BOLD FARMER HEAVILY FINED FOR CkIELTY TO ANIMALS.

At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs, S. Taylor and T. Pilkington, John Pemberton, farmer, Bold. was charged with causing a horse to be illtreated, on the 11th March and Thomas Nightingale was ebarg.l with working the earne whilst in an unfit state. Pemberton was also charged with having, on the 12th March, illtreated a horse by neglecting to give it proper care and attention: else with cruelly illtreating a horse by neglecting to supply it with sufficient food and nourishment.—Mr. Swift appeared on behalf of the prosecution, and Mr. Marsh represented the defendauts.—Mr. Swift, after reading the Act of Parliament, acid that the defendant, John Pemberton, wan a farrner, and reaided at Bold. Upon the 11th of March his farm was visited by one of the officers of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. The officer there found the defendant Nightingale in • field, ploughing with two horses, one of thence Week mare ; and it was to that horse that the first two summonses referred. That black mare had on its near shoulder two wounds, each of the siaa oft florin, and on the off shoulder a third vrot,nd of the mole size. They were old wounds, and the collar was pressing on them, causing the animal great pain. Nightingale was spoken to, and he said that they had been sore for some titne. The defendant Pem- berton seeing them in the field, went to thorn, and the officer said to Pemberton, "Why do you nerd these ho. toes to work in this state?" Pemberton repli.l, al came over to see that there was nothing wrong with them ; I did not know the shoulders were to bad. I is ill not work her till she is better: I hope you will lotik over it this time." The officer saw several animals, beside the black mare. which deserved his attention and when he returned to his head quarters, he report.' what he had seen, and, in consequence at his report, the local secretary of the society and the 90Cikly.A local veterinary surgeon paid a aecond visit to the farm on the following day; and there they found a black gelding in a deplorable condition, very weak ant emaciated. It had an injured knee, from which it was suffering acute pain.and was not able to put its foot on the ground. There was a contuaed wound the size of a man's hand on the nur loin, and another on the near shoulder and the left eye was closed owing to a contusion on the upper part of it. The aninral was skin and bane. Pemberton said that the horse wee not working, but was simply out to stretch her legs a bit. So that it was quite clear that it had been in that can- dition some time without advice or assistance. There was also a brown mare Mich was in a very poor condition. It was drawing a pinup, and appeared very hungry ; it could scarcely move along, not was weak, emaciated, and totally unfit for neck. Th. accused said, alt is old, and old horses are bad to keep in condition ; I give them Indian corn and Ocean." The officer looked over the premises and could not find any provender—corn or bran hut he found a little very bad bay only fit for litter. The officer told Pemberton that the fact was he had not given them sufficient food and Pemberton in reply said that "hr had been very unlucky a short time ago his byres were burnt down, and all the fodder and corn he had Wee deatroyal. Therefore he had not got it to give them, and hoped they would forgive and not summons him." There could be no doubt whatever of that man's cruelty to those animals. They could have made separate and distinct charges with regard to other animals but they did not want to be oppressive, but simply to show people float they must deal with some show of humanity to dumb animals. Pemberton himself had been convicted no less than three times under that Act of Parliament for cruelty to his animals ; and if they fouud the case proved he hoped they would have no hesitation as to the course they ought to take with Oman who, after three warnings, after three iffinvictione. allowed his animals to remain on his farm, and to be in his service in such a condition as he (Mr. Swift) had stated to their worships.—Mr. 3W. Motutn, the local secretary to the society, and Mr. A. Blein, veter- inary surgeon, gave evidence as to the state the animals were in when visited by them, and bearing out Mr. Swift's statements—Mr. Marsh, for the defence, called Thomas Quinn, who has resided with Mr. Pemberton, the defendant for three years, and who said that he fed the horses all alike, three times a day, on a chopped hay, rolled India, and bran." The brown mare had only her. working a few days as she had only recently cast her foale—The Bench said they thought the case a very bad one, and they would give the defendant the full penalty in every case—£s and costs. Nightingale would be line] 10s, and cotta—As the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animale receives no monies half of the amount was ordered to be given to the Cottage Hospital.

Thomas Hardman, a married man, apparently about 27 years of age. whom wife and two children reside in Wales, was charged with indecently assaulting a little girl name,' Annie Toole, about ten years of age. who resides with her mother in Langtree-street, in Farr —Mr...Swift appeared on behalf of the complainant. and Mr. Riley for the defendant.—From the evidence of the prosecution, it appear.' that defendant hod lodged at complainant's mother's house for six months. Complainant, on Sat urday. suggested to Mrs. Toole that she should go to St. Helens to do her marketing, and that he and the girl would take charge of the house during her absence. The Brother trent to an adjacent shop to get some provisions before going to the market. Defendant then told the girl logo upstairs to make the beds, but she declined and he then acted in an indecent manner. The mother came in shortly after, and found the little girl black in the face and frothing at the mouth. She remonstrated with the de- , fendsnt, who shnply sahl that be had been playing with the - child. Leyland, who met with his death on Thursday afternoon, at the St. Helens Collieries, Sutton. It app.red that the deceased, who was married, went to his work, in the morning usual, at the Rushy Park Mire. In the middle of the Afternoon, about three tons of dirt fell upon him, whilst he was working in an endwav in the lower level of the mine. A mut named Kilshaw had been work- ing with bion, but h.t left for about ten minutes to fetch an empty box and on returning seeing the roof bid fallen, he shouted for Leyland, but receiving no answer, he called the underlooker, who ordered the man to be extricated from the debris. Ile was found to be quite dead, and woc at once re- moved Co 74, Claughton-street, where he resided. Sr. HELENA —The Hight Rev. Bishop Kelly held • confirmation service in St. Thomas's Church on Wednesday at three o'clock in the afternoon. There were present the Rev. J. C. Pigot, the vicar, the Rev. C. J. Yong°, curate, and the Rev. S. Wilkin- son, of Warrington. The church was crowded wtth people anxious to see the ceremony; and the police had to use a very ingenious method to get the contirmeee into the church and avoid the undue pressure of the crowd. One hundred and sixty-nine presented themselves for confirmation—lY males and 73 ferrules. Two or three of the males were elderly persoss. The Bishop pointed out the importance of the step they had taken, and urged upon them to read a por- tion of the scriptures daily. After the service tea was pro- aided the school-room, Lyon-street; and in the evening a service win held, at which the contirmees were present. The Rev. J C. Young preached a very appropriate sermon. Tee WESLEYAN Tirawasoivtwo Forn.—Thr. President of the Wesleyan Conference, the Rev. B. Gregory, has issued special letter on the Thanksgiving Fund, in order to remove an impression that prevails that, as the promises to the Thanksgiving Fund already exceed the amount which its promotem ventured to name at first, the necessity is superseded for an effort of liberality on the part of circuits whose Thanksgiving Fund meetings have not yet been held corresponding with that so auspiciously put forth by those who took the initiative, and those by whom the style and standard of generosity have hitherto been so nobly sustained. The President points out" the mistaken. ness and untimeliness of any such idea," as the highest figure to which the fund could be raised by a liberality even exceeding that which has already hero evinced must !still, he says, fall very far short of she existing and argent necessities of Methodism. The absolute requirements of the three great departments—the Foreign Missions, the Theological Institution, with its new establishment in Birmingham, and the Schools Fund—would alksoth any amount that can be reached by the most enthusiastic exer- tions. The fund has now reached £289,358 111 s. 9d.

Smut:Mtn AcMonte'r kr Sr. HELENS Juserrote.— Yesterday afternoon a man named Samuel Lethwell, of At, Exeler-stieet, Ardwick, met with a rather singalar but serious accident. It appears that he left St. Helens by the 335 p.m train for Mancheater, yin the Junction. On arriv- ing at the latter place be left the company's premises aad proceeded to an hotel near, where he had some drink. Shortly after returning to the station he was found in a pool of blood, in the waiting-room, close to the fender. He was raised, when blood was found to be ' rapidly oozing out from the back of his bead and neck. The St. Ilelens stationmaster (Mr. Moss) was immediately telegraphed to meet the man and render as. sietance, as lie would be forwarded the neat train. On his arrival he was assisted by two railway officials and Police- sergeant 201 to the residence of the company's surgeon, a few hundred yards from the station. A complete line of blast war formed from the atation to the surgery and the man's clothes were quite saturated. 1/r. Brown examined the man, and found that several arteries were severed in the head and neck. The wounds were immediately dressed and the arteries tied up. lie was again asisted to the station, and sent to Manchester by the 6-20 train. It is supposed that tree man fell on the edge of the fender, and es injured himself. After being attended to by the doetor—whe received much abuse from his patient during the operation— the man composedly asked a by-stander to accompany him to public-bouseand have a "drain.'

Hour, RAINHILL.—The anniversan tea party in connec- tion with the Sunday school, was held in the school room, on Wedneeday last. About 120 sat down to tea. which, (supplied by Mr. Seddon) consisted of the usual good thing.: and gave every satisfaction. After tea an entertainment prodded over by O. lb. Rawlins, Esq., Rainhill, was given by the scholars and passed off most successfully. The following programme was gone through, and the audience by their hearty reception of the performers showed their appreciations of the efforts made for their amusement Opening hymn, "We all can do something for Jeer."; song and chorus, "Ring the bell, watchman"; dialogue, "'The good old times"; song, "Thy voice is near"; recitation, "The chameleon"; song and chorus, "Little sister's gone to sleep"; recitation, "Folly"; hymn, "Don't you been the angels "; eong and chorus, "theil bleu our sailor Prince " ; dialogue, "Father come home "; song and chorus, "Father pray with me to-night"; recitation, "Signs of rein" ; wog, " Mother kiteed me in my dream "; solo and chorus, " Jeer save the Queen' Mr. Jones (Whiston) moved, and Mr. Welch (Rafnhill) seconded, a vote of thanks to the Chairman, who, in reply, expressed his satisfaction at the good work done by the school for the neighbourhood. A vote of thanks, moved by Mr. Ames (Prescott and seconded by Mr. Stoba (Huyten), concluded the proceedings. During the entertainment the room vas crowded to excess, and advantage had hobo taken of every inch of space to accommodate the audience. Alto- gether the committee may he complimented upon having given the utmost satisfaction to all present, and gained eomething towards the funds of the school.

SHIPPING THADE.—The lung-continued depression in the shipping trade of Liverpool seems effect to be about to pass away, and arcing hopes are entertained that a better state of things will now pre- vail. There is especial activity in the American trade, as it is instanceal by the fact that during the past week no fewer than thirteen largo s.ainers left the Mersey for the United States and Canada with heavy cargoes and large numbers of emigrants. THE ftaisn CATTLE IMPORT THADE.—II is interesting to : find see time when every effort is being made to develcpe , the American cattle trade that there is a tendency in the , direction el iner.sing our cattle imports from Ireland. Al- ready • very large number of cattle come from Belfast to Barrow, hut it has teen found necessary to open up a direct cattle trade between Dundalk and Barrow. With the view of encouraging the trade the Corporation of Barrow have doter- mined to open a new cattle market at Barrow.

A.I.OAIiATED SoCIETIC Or CARPENTERS ono JOINNIM.— Ile twentieth annual report of this society, just issued, states that the deptession experienced in the building trade during 1879 has been unparalleled within the memory of the present generation, the expenditure having been increased by nearly £lB,OOO more than in the previous year. The total of disbursements woe £62,446 ; and, under the circum- stances, the society sustained a loss during the year of £12,591. The value of the newts were, however, £53,590, and a more prosperoua year was anticipated. The receipts amounted ta £39,854,. decrease of £1.734. The total sum paid to unemployed members was £27,902, that being £1 12s. Dd. per metnber, and increase of £1 Or. Id. per mem- ber upon the expenditure of 1878. The eociety also grants , sick benefit, and in this £ll,OOB has been spent ; and makes allowances for superannuation, funeral, loss of tools, he. The total number of members was at the end of the year , 17,034, an increase of 430 °ye. 1879. 1 loon ant, SYner..—At a recent meeting of the Society of Telegraph Engineers, Professor Hughes read a paper tilted" Note on some effects produced by the immersion of iron and steel wires in acidulated waters," in which were shown aome very remarkable effects of the action of acids on iron and stool wires. It was shown that the mere dip- ping of a piece of iron wire in sulphuric acid rendered it highly brittle, and gave it many of the characters of steel. Professor Hughes also showed that iron used in conjunction with sine in a single fluid cell made one of the most con- Mont batteries known, and was almost entirely free from the disturbing effect. of polarisation.—A discussion took place, doting which Mr. Chandler Roberts announced the fact that Ire had succeeded in extracting hydrogen of 20 times the voluthe of the iron in whic'i it was occluded or absorbed, thus showing an intimate connection between hydrogen and the brittleness of the wire. The opinion seemed to be pretty general that we were on the right track to form tome idea as to the reason of that strange alteration which renders it steel.

---(-3iITTON TRADE IN Csaans..—A writer in a Canadian newspaper, referring to the cotton trade in Canada, say, : " We are only at the threshold of good times, and yet the increase of the demand for cotton goods has been no great that every spindle has been working overtime except when a pause has bern compellel for lack of raw cotton. lit course some of thin activity is due directly to the new tariff, which has excluded son), descriptions of foreign goods, but it is mostly doe to a genuine revival of demand. Short as hae been the time since the denmnd sprang up, and great as were the clocks in the manufacturers' hands, the supply is already insufficient, and many a trader who would willingly fill his shelves finds that he is utterly unable to procure the goods. It is probable that in the goal times which are coming Canada will consume thirty yards per head per annum. Thie will be 120,000,060 yards for our whole popu- lation. We have mille which will supply only 28,000,000 yards. It is quite possible that in some lines dm production is equal to the demand in slack timers but at the present time the proluction is notoriously not equal to the denland, and the new mills will, we undet stand, address themselves to new descriptionn of goods. The effect of all this is that, notwithstanding protection ranging from 25 to 50 per cert., wholesale merchants will be compelled to in)port cottons in order to keep their trade and protect themselvee against the coming rise in paces. As eosin am ever there has to be im- ported cottons of the qualities made in Canada, the prices of the whole of the home manufactured product will rise to that of the imported plea the duty. We shall then be pay- ing 30, 40, and 50 per cent, of taxation on an article which we need to get at 17i per cent." WAG. IN one COTTON TNALl6.—Torimorden: The wagel dispute at Der-street Shed (Mesas. Firth and Clarke's) has now been settled, after a fortnight's strike, the weavers hav- ing resumed work, and the masters having granted an advance of wage. of nearly 5 per cent. An advance to the same extent has been eubmitted to by the masters of Cinderhill Mill, Castle-street. The operative. of Messrs. Lord Brothere, of Stackhills and Canal-street, are still out on strike, in con- sequence of the master, refusing to advance wages. For • few daye past eopport has been asked for ill various quarters, and on Saturday the weavereattended at one of the rooms of the Co-operative Society, Dale-etreet, to receive s share of the money collected the operatives received 2s. per loom a, a result of the appeal made to the operatives who are in work in the town. The weavers of Messrs. Barker. and Crabtree, of Crow-care, logs, and Wadsworth Mill, Todraorden, are still out on strike, owing to the masters declining to advance wages One per cent, at present, and five per cent. in July. The dispute has lasted over a week, while that at Lord Brother.' has now been going on towards a month. At Wadsworth Mill alterations are going on which it will take two or three weeks to complete, but the hande express them- selves as determined not to renew their eng.rgement unless an advance is conceled.—lilecAlksa: Meetings of weavers were held at 108 mills in Blackburn on Monday to consider the data of the threatened strike for an advadce of wage.. Deputies were appointed at the ratio of one for each 400 looms, and these reported at a meeting held at the Spinners' Institute on Monday night, when 80 presented themrelves. After a somewhat stormy discussion, it appeared that 53 deputies were in favour of striking at Whiteuntideas recoup mended by the wage, committee for North and North-east Lancashire, unless the advance be conceled, while 22 were in favour of coming out at once. Tan Come T.D.—Farmers hare offere,l English wheat very sparingly both at Mark Lane and in the country markets, and it le evident that the reserves of last year's crop are extremely small. Although the condition has been fair, the quality oi the majority of the samples have been no indifferent that sales have been exceedingly difficult to effect, and the range ol price, has been no extended that a difference of about 20s. per quarter exists between the high- est and Igwest gootttiens. The cheapest parcels to millers have evrdently been the highest priced, es they have steadily ignored the existence of inferior produce. The trade hen been quiet, and line parcels of home-grown have found buvere at previone rates, the decline on foreign not having affected Englieh corn. Really fine indigenous wheat is now getting extremely scarce, no that the bulk sf the milling demand, which has shown signs of improvement during the week, has fallen on foreign, of which the imports, both actual and prospective, have been too large to enable sellers to establieh any advance. All varieties have moved into consumption with steadiness, if not freedom, at last Monday', decline of la ed. per quarter on American, and le. per quarter on Russian sorts. It must be remembered that in spite of the collapse of the wheat " ring " ia America, and the consequent release of the accumulated stocks on the Atlantic eeaboard, the actual etatistical position of the trade is unchanged, and that the abundance on the other side will not more than counterbalance deficiency on this between now and harvest. Of course prices may, and probably will, be influenced by 0 bull " and " bear " operation, in the leading American grain centres, bat the principal element of consideration ill the future will be the action of the weather on the growing crops of the Old and New World. The trade closed dull at the end of the week, and a furthm reduction was necessary to effect sales of both wheat and maize. The reles of F-nglish wheat noted last week were 27,586 quarters, at 47e. lid., against 47.640 quarters, at 41s. 21. in the previous year. The London Average for the week ending April 15th was 44e. Out, on 1,184 quarters. The imports into the United Kingdom for the week ending April 10th were 1,328,799 cwt, of wheat and 174.368 cwt. of dour.

GREAT SEIZURE OF SurOOLIM TOBACcO.—An exteneive seizure of smuggled tobacco was made on Thursday in and , near Hull. Late on Wednesday night • police constable watched the premises of a wholesale tobacconist in Hall named Robert l'uolson. He aaw a van drive up to a shed at the 1 rear of the shop, and suspecting it containdl smuggled goods he took two men who were in chargeof it into custody. They were sons of l'oulson, who was also apprehended. A box and two racks were discovered in the van, containing about 150Ib. of contraband tobacco. The Custom-house officiale were communicated with, and from information they re- ceived officers were sent off to watch Poulson's private residence, about four miles from the town, and also a sus- pected locality on the banks of the Humber. On Thurs- day morning nearly 60 balesof tobacco--each bale containing about SOM.—were found in • garden at the back of l'oulson'e boom. The officers watching on the river side also made. extensive seisure about the same time. Seeing • boat they went towards it, when three men nuddenly made their ap- pearance and ran away. fhe officers gave chase and caught two of them, one of whom, however, afterwards escaped. Twenty sacks of tobacco were found in the boat, and a similar quantity was discoverer' in • baton the river side. Altogether the quantity seized amounts to over 5,011a11b. Six men and a bonnet already in custody. They were brought before the magistrate on Thursday and remanded. his. GnuYrer said' I do not know whether it is necessary in proposing • chairman to say anything with regard to the duties devolving upon the person occoping the office. Without further remarks, I volt mope. that Mr. William Derbyshire be elected chairnian for the ensuing year. Under all the circum- stances, I think he is in every way fitted for the office. He has highly commended himself to us for his shrewdness, good common ammo, and honesty. Major Carcrwalutay, I Indn about to epeek just before ME Harrison rose, as I had a word or two to say with regard to the late senior vice-chairman and this appointment. SHOCKING DEAfII 101.' A WO3IAN AT WARRINGTON.

An inquest was held at the Feathers Inn, Bridge-street, on Thursday, by the deputy coroner, Mr. T. W. Barker, on the baly of Mrs. Mary Ellison, who resided at Friars' Gate, and who died under the following circumstances. The coroner in addressing the jury add, there seemed to hire to be very disgraceful conduct on the part of the brother, but they would hear the evidence and probably express some opinion on his conduct. ." • • ' • •• • • ' " •

thomae Wehrleley, mid helloed at 11 Friaes'-gate and wee a farm labourer. The deceased was his siWer and was 50 years of age. Her name was Mary Ellimn, and she Ira, the widow of William Ellison, late of Fenketh, general labourer. He had lived with the decemied since her hueband'e death, and for the Lest twelve months at 11 Friars ,gate. Deceased had a stroke of palsy twelve month. last July and had not been very strong aince. On Friday last deceased wais worse. She came down stair, with his help about 10 o'clock, when she complained of being weak. Ile got her some gruel and she seemed better. Fir was with her all Friday and made her some beef tea which !she took with .t little egg. On Satur- day she was worse, but would not lion,. lector. He was in and out all day on Saturday. Deceased had two wine alam tulle of whiskey, with a little water. She remained on the sofa from Friday, as deceased said she did not want to go up stairs. On Sunday morning he went to Bank Quay to gee nmoanieee deceased mooted to be a little better,and he was away about quarter 01 .0 hour. Ile returned before 10 o'clock,and was in the house all day. He went to get some whiskey about 8 o'clock in the evening, and was taken into custody shortly aftemards teethe Bose and Crown public house. There W. plenty of food in the house beef, eggs, bread, and potatoes. D.weased had been in the habit of taking drink for 12 menthe to hie k,nowledge. He last raw his sister time about 7.30 on Stunlay evening when he went out—fly the jury: Whenever he left home he took the key of the door with him, because the deceased wished him to do no. He did not think she would have "popped off so mon as Om did. There was no disturbance between them on Saturday night. Mrs. Sarah Have, sffil she had known the &relined for about 18 months. She was a very drunken wotnan, and the last witness wad elm fond of drink, but not we louder deceased was. She never knew the brother to um arty violence, and there was no disturbance that she knew of the last two or three days. She saw the deceased about one o'clock on Sunday, when Dr. Smith was there. Deceased seemed very weak and only juet alive. She never heard deceased complain of any ac.. of violence on the part of any- one. She saw deceased again about half-pant five, when ehe saw her on the door insensible. She got deceased up, and she drank a little tea. The brother would not allow anyone in the house unless he was Chore. Ile made use of bad language. and she could not stay. She new Walmesley lock the Ileum about balf.past seven. The relieving °dicer came about half-part nine and got the key, and on witness going in she found deceased dead on the sofa, in the same poeition ae she last eaw her.—lty the Jury: Deceased wan ill about eight weeks last summer, when Walmesley attended her like a woman. _

—ii,:7'11;;;;;;11;rbourne, relieving officer, said he was mint for hr note about six o'clock on Sunday night last. Ile went to the ileceasnl's house. The brother opened the door, and he was then the worse for drink. Deceaned was lying on the sofa in the kitchen. She was unconscious. He put some questions to the brother, who said she had eaten nothing for three days, but had been drinking, and showed him a bottle of whiskey. Deceased opponent to be dying, and he went for Dr. Spinks and the police. He came back with the chief constable, but found the door was locked. They went to the Hose and Crown public-house, where they found the brother drunk. Mr. Hunt searched hint and took !din into custody. They returned to the house and found the deceased dead. There was food in the house and the brother had plenty of money. Dr. Starkey Smith deposed that on Sunday afternoon last about a quarter to three, he was walking down the street when he was called by the deceased's brother, who wanted him tore to gee his s'ister. He (the brother) woe very ad- vanced in drink at the time. He found the deceased lying partially on chairs and partially on a couch. He did. not think she had sufficient clothing, but she made no cow. plaint. The brother did nothing but swear. He (witness) then left and communicated with the police. On Monday he, with Dr. Spinks' made a post-mortem examination. There wan no external mark except a slight bruise on the I I knee, which might have been CAllAfti by a fall to the floor. Internally the body was well nourished. The brain washard, land the left ventricle contained a large quantity of serum. The heart was over-loaded with fat, and there was fatty degeneration. The liver was in the state known as " gin drinker's liver," through drinking large quantities of spirits. There wee not the least trace of food in lier eyetem, and It was their opinion that she had not had any solid food for three or four days. The general appearance of the body was that of a pereon addicted to habits of intemperance for a long period. He thought death had occurred from weak action of the heart and from emits apoplexy. The Coroner, in summing up, mid he was glad to find that the evidence the jury had had put a very different aspect upon the matter than that which it at firut aeaumed. It appeared that the unfortunat- woman had contributed to her death by her own habits. There was no legal obligation upon the brother to look after the deceased, and they found he wan only a ledger; but it was adisfactory to find that the man had belT•ed well to her. The lucking of the door was a suspicions item in the case, but that was explained. He (the Coroner) thought the jury might come to the con- clarion that on the whole there was no want of core on the part of anyone, neither was them any violence on the part 0 anyone. The jury returned an open verdict in accordance with the medical evidence, and, at their requeet,the Coroner censured the brother for his disgraceful conduct towards the doctor . .

SALE. CON'EUIVATEVE ASSOCIATION EDE SALE AND DISESICT.— At a meeting held on Monday night in the Brooklands Private Club, it was decided to establish a Conservative and ; Constitutional Association for Sale, Ashton-on-Mersey, and the district. The meeting was very numerously attended. 11 and the proposal was tairen up with a spirit which augurs well for the success of the new association, Mr. J. Ingrain prodded, and among other gentlemen present were fir. Hoyle, Mr. W. E. Joynson, and Mr. N. Kilvert. It was stated that 100 persons, including a goodly number of tenant farmers, had promised to join the association, and that the ' proprietom of the Brookland Private Club had offered the um of their premises until a permanent borne be obtained for the association. A considerable number of those present intimated their readiness to becon.e members, and there is every prospect of the organisation entering upon its exis- tence with a nucleus of large proportions. The want of such an association has long been felt in the district, and .1 50 time more than during the late election. This has sti.nulatel the Conservativea to action, and it is to be hoped that they will not rest satisfied until they have established a powerful electoral agency as well as a good social club.

Coals for ship- ment have been meeting with rather better inquiry. The borne demand, however, is generally very snail, and there, a good deal of underselling to secure orders. The average quoted prices at the pit mouth are 81. to In. ad. per ton for best house coal, Ba. to os. !Id. for seconds, and On. to ss. 6!, for common round coal. Bd., with 4s. ftd, per ton being asked in some cases.— In the iron trade of this distriot them has borne very depressed tone during the past week, and there has been a continued downward movement in values to an extent that has taken evsryone by surprise, whilst second-hand hold of iron anxious to realise have become so alarmed that thee have endeavoured :o force sales at almost any figure Of coarse, the unfavourable reports received frost the other markets have materially added to the depression here, and there has been an almost entire abeence of demand, with very little inquiry, both dealers and consumers, in the face of the downward movement in prices, refusing to give out ordere at present. it appeared the prisoner', father W 34 a publican, and made an independency, and the prisoner's sister married 111. named Ellison, who was possess& of money, which, although he had a large family. he left to his wife. Mr. Ellison died, and since that time he had lived with his sister, on Friar's- I green. During the last week stricter or ill and several persons went to see her, but the prisoner sent them hack. The prisoner, when drunk, stopped Dr. Smith, and told hint he was wanted to see Mrs. Ellison. Mr. Harboutne, the relieving officer, got to hear of the case, and went to the house and toned Mrs. Elliman in a dying elate, but the prisoner was very abusive, and Mr. Hunt was sent for The prisoner, however, had left the house, but he was found drunk at the Rose and Crown with a glass ef beer before hint, cede bottle of whiskey in his pocket. The Chief con- stable asked the prisoner for the key of the house, but he re- fused to produce it. It Wes, however, obtained from him and on going to the house Mrs. Ellison was found to be dead on a couch. The woman appeared to have been neg- lected, for although there was food in the house it was un- cooked and there was no fire. Ile believed the woman lay three or four days on the floor inc helpless state Mr. Har- bourne said the house her! a very cleanly appearance, and was well furnished, its condition was eomewhat inconsistent with the habits of the priaoner and his sister. Mrs. Ellison had for a considerable time been given to drink, living more upon it than on food. Ile made the necessary enquiries and wrote to the coroner advising an inquest and the post mortem examinntion. The prisoner bad never worked for his living, but had been living with his sister for some years, and there was a question as to the advisibility of allowing the prisoner to he at large.—The prisoner, who said be had dune his best far his sister as long as lethal ever been able to look after her., ns remanded until Thursday._ .. Tea dramas or Toe STRETFORD GAS CONMeNT.—At the Salford Quarter Sesaions, on Monday, a petition was pre- sented to the Court on behalf of Mr. Charles Anthony Surgliardt, of Srooklands, hicturer on mineralogy to Owens College, and Mr. Algal' Suss., Stretford, repreaentatives of the Stretford the Consumers' Vigilance Committee, praying for the appointment by the court of on auditor to examine the accounts of the Stretford the Company, with a view to obtain, after the auditor should have presented hie rep rt, an order for the reduction in the price of the gas charged by the company.—Mr. S. Taylor, who appeared for the petitioners, said lie made the application under the 33th section 00th. Gee Work Clauses Act, IS-17. Mr. Nash, who appeared for the Oa, Company, was, he understood, prepared to consent to the order which was desired. What he (Mr. Taylor) there- ' fore applied for was the appointnient of an accountant to go through the books of the company. Such accountant would be agreni upon between the parties; the trouble therefore of Inning upon a gentleman to examine the books would not I devolve upon the court.—Mr. Nash mid he practically con- sented to the application made by the Vigilance Committee. —Mr. Higgin. What is that o—Me. Nash stated that the con, mittee in question was, he understood, composed of cerMin gas consumers at Stretford, who complained of the price which the company charged for gas. He himself lived at Stretford, and had had no reason to complain of the price. The compauy desirni to show that they nere not opimsed to any fair examination and investigation of their accounts. On the contrary, they were anxious to assist in the prosecu- tion of the investigation, and would facilitate it.—Mr. liiggin toed. paragraph in the petition, from which he add he gathered the petitioners complained that the consumers were overcharged, and that money had been paid to the share- holders which, uzder the provisiona of the Act of Parlia- ment, they were not entitled to receive.—The court granted the application, and Mr. Aldred, accountant, Dickinson- street, Manchester, was appointed to examine the books of the company,
